We describe and evaluate a three-way merge in which the schema defines a conflict: set algebra combines canonical triples, and a slot is contended only where a SHACL shape bounds its cardinality and both sides' changes cannot stand within that bound. Unbounded predicates union; contended slots go to a person. The same shapes graph validates the result. We do not claim the first three-way merge for RDF. Our contribution is an implementation in a production multi-agent store and an evaluation against a reimplementation of Quit Store's Context Merge overlap rule, which it extends rather than replaces, and six other strategies. Across five synthetic seeds, the shape-aware operator raised 33 conflicts, all true positives as judged by the same shapes that define them, with no triples lost or fabricated and no SHACL violations admitted. The context-overlap baseline, counted per slot, detected the same 33 conflicts but asked 845 questions. A replay built from recorded production incidents covers 105 human alias repairs (93 after excluding 12 chained pairs) and 939 duplicate-value incidents. It reproduces a triple-level limit: different names for one entity remain invisible (0 of 93 alias repairs detected, matching 0 of 21 synthetic cases). In a study of evolving shape contracts, merging shape declarations first handles the tested cardinality changes, while datatype evolution exposes a detector blind spot caught by post-merge validation. An oracle that reads no shapes agrees with the shipped operator on the facts and history of all 23 reachable single-slot cases. Under wrong shapes, a missing bound loses data silently and a spurious one only adds questions. The supported claim is fewer human decisions with nothing silently lost, for cardinality conflicts in one deployment, not general merge correctness.

authors.name: Steve Brown

papers.title: How Much Do Coding Agents Over-Edit, and Why? An Empirical Study of Unneeded Edits in Repository-Level Agent Patches
papers.summary: Agent patches are larger than developers', which is widely read as over-editing. But patch size does not say whether the extra edits are needed, what they are, or where they come from. We introduce Delta Residue Attribution (DRA), which replays agent trajectories, traces every block (unit) of the final patch to the step that wrote it, reverts each unit, and reruns the task tests to decide whether the unit is needed. We apply DRA to 7,660 resolved GitHub Copilot CLI trajectories from 18 frontier models on SWE-bench Verified (6,728) and DeepSWE (932), and grade developer patches using the same method. Agent patches do change more lines than developers'; on SWE-bench Verified the majority of extra edits add tests (61%) and documentation (13%) while on DeepSWE, most extra edits are code (58%). On both benchmarks, agents' code is on average at least as necessary as developers' (mean $NP_{code}$ 0.887 vs. 0.864 on SWE-bench Verified, where 11 of 18 models leave less unneeded code than developers, and 0.797 vs. 0.785 on DeepSWE). On average, 11% of an agent patch's code units on SWE-bench Verified are still unneeded, and 89% of those change behavior. Debug steps write almost none of the unneeded code. Code necessity differs substantially by model; it is unrelated to resolve rate on SWE-bench Verified and negatively correlated with it on DeepSWE (Spearman -0.59, p = 0.01). On SWE-bench Verified, pruning with DRA using only the tests the agent can see (its own tests and the repository's) removes the majority of unneeded code but also some needed code (67% recall, 46% precision), and 89% of pruned patches still resolve the task; asking the agent to audit its own diff is more precise but less effective (36% recall, 66% precision). We recommend that benchmarks report code necessity next to resolve rate and that over-editing be addressed through model training and harness-level pruning.

authors.name: Aakash Goel, Benjamin Steenhoek, Yu Hu

papers.title: Interpretable and Accurate Hybrid Decision Trees with Selective Case-Based Splits
papers.summary: Decision trees are among the most well-known interpretable models in Machine Learning. Over the years, a wide variety of strategies have been proposed to define split conditions within the greedy learning framework, aiming to guide instance routing and enhance predictive performance. These strategies range from axis-parallel and oblique splits based on feature values to proximity-based splits using exemplar instances and more complex hybrid approaches. However, no single method has emerged as universally superior. In this work, we present two key contributions to the construction of greedy decision trees. First, we propose a hybrid tree architecture that integrates both feature-based and case-based splits, allowing for heterogeneous splits throughout the tree. Second, we introduce a novel type of split that leverages a selective case-based approach: when a split is needed, our method searches for the most informative subset of features to define the split, effectively balancing the specificity of case-based methods with the simplicity of feature-based ones. Experiments on a diverse set of tabular datasets show that our method outperforms standard decision trees and achieves performance on par with ensemble methods, while producing shallow trees that retain or even improve predictive accuracy.

authors.name: Cristiano Landi, Alessio Cascione, Riccardo Guidotti

papers.title: Enhancing Maritime Domain Awareness using Latent Space Representations
papers.summary: This work presents a novel application of Earth Observation (EO) embeddings for Maritime Domain Awareness (MDA) from the perspective of the geospatial foundation model TerraMind. By operating directly on compressed latent-space representations rather than on the original Sentinel-1 imagery, this approach directly addresses the data gravity bottleneck that increasingly constrains operational EO processing, in line with the objectives of the Embed2Scale project. In particular, linear and non-linear probing of compressed embeddings, latent space representations of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery, is used to detect, localise, and characterise vessels from Sentinel-1 GRD images. Vessel detection achieves a ROC-AUC of 0.95, while vessel localisation has a median error of around 300 m for vessels longer than 100 m, and vessel AIS type-code classification achieves 62% accuracy for the majority classes. The latter, however, is highly correlated with vessel length. These results reveal both the potential and current limitations of Geospatial Foundation Models (GeoFMs) when applied to fine-grained MDA understanding in real-world scenarios. Additionally, a new maritime remote sensing dataset is released, pairing about 2,000 Sentinel-1 images with temporally aligned AIS signals from commercial vessels. Through manual inspection, each candidate sample was verified for bounding-box quality and for consistency between the AIS-reported vessel length and the observed vessel extent, cross-checking vessel identity and location against publicly available vessel records and, where available, photographs. The dataset was made ready for use with the NeuCo-Bench neural compression benchmark framework, publicly available on HuggingFace through https://huggingface.co/datasets/embed2scale/S1-single-ship-downstream .

authors.name: Rikard Vinge, Miguel A. Belenguer-Plomer, Isabelle Wittmann, Octavian Dumitru, Michele Lazzarini, Sergio Albani, Conrad M Albrecht

papers.title: $\mu$-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-User Task Completion in Shared Interaction Voice Agents
papers.summary: Voice agents in shared spaces must satisfy interdependent multi-user requests while upholding per-user authority, privacy, and task constraints. Existing evaluations offer limited coverage when participants react throughout a session. We introduce $\mu$-Bench, a benchmark for joint task completion in closed-loop, full-duplex multi-user voice interaction. Simulated participants act from isolated profiles of goals, knowledge, and permissions, adapting to the agent's speech and tool outcomes. Across 20 domains, 100 scenarios vary group size, acoustics, and follow-up demands to form 800 cases (408 tool-augmented, 392 tool-free). Joint Task Success (JTS) requires all user goals, privacy boundaries, and terminal states to hold jointly, while Pure JTS further disallows unauthorized tool calls; Attribution, Threading, and Coordination (ATC) diagnostics localize failures. Across 13 voice agents, proprietary systems peak at 62.24\% tool-free and 65.44\% tool-augmented success, while open-weight models remain below 20\%. ATC diagnostics show that open-weight models lag primarily in multi-turn attribution and threading, and controlled contrasts reveal that larger groups consistently degrade joint task success across capable systems. By coupling reactive multi-user simulation with verifiable session-level outcomes, $\mu$-Bench provides a rigorous testbed for shared voice agents.

authors.name: Qihao Lin, Guanxu Chen, Shuhang Zheng, Xiaoya Lu, Jingyi Yang, Terumi Chiba, Wenyi Yu, Chao Zhang, Zhuan Shi, Jing Shao

papers.title: Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces for Hard Math Problems
papers.summary: Post-training large language models (LLMs) for mathematical reasoning often relies on accepted traces whose final answers pass a verifier. For hard math problems, however, such traces can be rare under independent Monte Carlo (MC) sampling. To address this, we propose Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces (DART), a trace-mining method that starts from a rejected trace, decomposes it into reasoning steps, and ranks them by position-weighted uncertainty. It then generates deliberately distinct alternative candidates for highly ranked steps using reference-answer guidance and a meta-thought before completing the resulting traces. On greedy-unsolved DeepMath-103K problems, DART recovers 37% more problems than MC sampling at a matched number of generated traces. Its estimated generation cost per recovered problem is nearly identical, while its cost per accepted trace is 30% lower. Post-training Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on traces mined by DART achieves the highest point estimate in five of six evaluations across MATH-500 and AIME benchmarks. These results demonstrate that revisiting rejected traces with DART can expand problem coverage and provide effective post-training data.

authors.name: Lukas Aichberger, Adam Golinski, Arno Blaas, Arwen Bradley, Jacob Springer, Mehrdad Farajtabar, Michael Kirchhof, Sinead Williamson

papers.title: Attack Policy Selection can Mislead Monitor Evaluators
papers.summary: AI monitors, classifiers that flag dangerous behaviour by AI agents, are often evaluated against transcripts generated by attack policies acting as proxies for dangerous behaviour in deployment. We evaluate an ex-production OpenAI monitor as a case study and find that measured false negative rate is highly sensitive to both the method used to generate attack policies and the level of optimisation applied within that method. This rate ranged from 0.5\% to 20.8\% across optimisation levels of a single method (reinforcement learning), and from 6.4\% to 23.0\% across methods at their best observed optimisation level (optimised prompting vs.\ transcript editing). Every attack policy was developed against proxy monitors only: all reported results show attacks transferring to the held-out GPT-5.4 target monitor. Our results suggest that monitor evasion evaluations can easily mislead: an evaluation using only basic attack methods may give false confidence that a monitor is strong. The sensitivity to attack-policy choice raises a problem: interpreting any particular result as evidence about deployment performance requires justification. The transcripts produced by attack policies are proxies for the dangerous behaviour a monitor must flag in deployment. These proxies can introduce visible artefacts, such as reasoning about a ``side task'' absent from the instructions shown to the monitor, that affect monitor judgements. Given the sensitivity above, the choice of proxy can change an evaluation's conclusion. Reading these results as evidence about deployment therefore requires a separate legitimacy argument for why the proxies are informative, including any justification of conservativeness. Making convincing arguments remains an open problem.

authors.name: Charlie Griffin, Oliver Makins, Asa Cooper Stickland, Alessandro Abate, Yarin Gal, Abby D'Cruz, Xander Davies

papers.title: Spectrum Adaptation of AI-Native Autoencoder Communications with Transfer Learning
papers.summary: End-to-end physical-layer learning replaces separate modulation, coding, and detection operations with an autoencoder (AE) that consists of a jointly trained encoder-decoder pair at the transmitter and the receiver. This paper studies AI-native communications with AEs and quantifies the sensitivity to training-test mismatch in channel models. Models trained only on an AWGN channel achieve low bit error rates (BERs) under matched conditions but degrade severely on Rayleigh fading with practical front-end impairments. To reduce the time and energy required to adapt to new channel conditions, we propose a low-latency transfer-learning procedure that starts from an AWGN-pretrained system and fine-tunes only a small subset of transmitter and receiver layers while freezing the remainder. We further formulate layer selection as a budget-constrained optimization problem that identifies the most informative parameters to update during adaptation. This preserves the learned signal geometry and the deep decision structure while adapting lightweight front ends to fading- and impairment-induced mixing. For AE communications, we show that partial updates remove the mismatch-induced error floor and approach the BER of fully retrained models. We provide a layer-wise study and quantify resource-performance trade-offs, showing that modest adaptation substantially reduces BER while cutting training time, multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations, energy consumption, and the fraction of updated parameters for resource-efficient implementation.

authors.name: Yalin E. Sagduyu, Tugba Erpek

papers.title: MathConstruct: Challenging LLM Reasoning with Constructive Proofs
papers.summary: While Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate impressive performance in mathematics, existing math benchmarks come with significant limitations. Many focus on problems with fixed ground-truth answers, and are often saturated due to problem simplicity or the viability of guessing or memorization. Crucially, they capture only a narrow subset of relevant math problems. To address this research gap, we introduce MathConstruct, a new benchmark of 121 challenging problems sourced from various math competitions, which targets constructive proofs, a widely encountered problem type requiring the construction of mathematical objects with specific properties. These proofs are particularly suitable for LLM evaluation, as solution correctness can be easily verified. Our automated verifiers also enable MathConstruct to generate problem variations, used to evaluate robustness. State-of-the-art LLMs solve only 60% of MathConstruct problems, highlighting its complexity and importance for LLM evaluation.

authors.name: Mislav Balunovi\'c, Jasper Dekoninck, Nikola Jovanovi\'c, Ivo Petrov, Martin Vechev

papers.title: MathArena: Evaluating LLMs on Uncontaminated Math Competitions
papers.summary: The rapid advancement of reasoning capabilities in large language models (LLMs) has led to notable improvements on mathematical benchmarks. However, many of the most commonly used evaluation datasets (e.g., AIME 2024) are widely available online, making it difficult to disentangle genuine reasoning from potential memorization. Furthermore, these benchmarks do not evaluate proof-writing capabilities, which are crucial for many mathematical tasks. To address this, we introduce MathArena, a new benchmark based on the following key insight: recurring math competitions provide a stream of high-quality, challenging problems that can be used for real-time evaluation of LLMs. By evaluating models as soon as new problems are released, we effectively eliminate the risk of contamination. Using this framework, we find strong signs of contamination in AIME 2024. Nonetheless, evaluations on harder competitions, such as CMIMC 2025, demonstrate impressive reasoning capabilities in top-performing models. MathArena is also the first benchmark for proof-writing capabilities. On IMO 2025, top models achieve slightly less than 40%, demonstrating both notable progress and significant room for improvement. So far, we have evaluated over $50$ models across seven competitions, totaling $162$ problems. As an evolving benchmark, MathArena will continue to track the progress of LLMs on newly released competitions, ensuring rigorous and up-to-date evaluation of mathematical reasoning.

authors.name: Mislav Balunovi\'c, Jasper Dekoninck, Ivo Petrov, Nikola Jovanovi\'c, Martin Vechev

papers.title: K12Vista: Exploring the Boundaries of MLLMs in K-12 Education
papers.summary: Multimodal large language models have demonstrated remarkable reasoning capabilities in various visual tasks. However, their abilities in K12 scenarios are still systematically underexplored. Previous studies suffer from various limitations including narrow subject coverage, insufficient data scale, lack of diversity in question types, and naive answer-centric evaluation method, resulting in insufficient exploration of model capabilities. To address these gaps, we propose K12Vista, the most comprehensive multimodal benchmark for Chinese K12 subject knowledge understanding and reasoning to date, featuring 33,000 questions across five core subjects from primary to high school and three question types. Moreover, beyond the final outcome, we are also concerned with the correctness of MLLMs' reasoning processes. For this purpose, we meticulously compiles errors from MLLMs' reasoning processes and leverage an automated data pipeline to construct K12-PEM-800K, the largest process evaluation dataset offering detailed step-by-step judgement annotations for MLLMs' reasoning. Subsequently, we developed K12-PEM, an advanced process evaluation model that integrates an overall assessment of both the reasoning process and answer correctness. Moreover, we also introduce K12-PEBench, the first high-quality, human-annotated benchmark specifically designed for evaluating abilities of reasoning process evaluation.Extensive experiments reveal that current MLLMs exhibit significant flaws when reasoning within K12Vista, providing critical insights for the development of more capable MLLMs.We open our resources at https://github.com/lichongod/K12Vista.

authors.name: Chong Li, Chenglin Zhu, Tao Zhang, Mingan Lin, Zenan Zhou

papers.title: Beyond Moral Performance: Empirical Assessment of LLMs' Moral Competence Through Judgment Stability
papers.summary: Evaluations of large language models (LLMs) have largely measured moral performance, whether their outputs are morally appropriate, rather than moral competence, the capacity to judge on the basis of morally relevant considerations. We test for competence by varying morally irrelevant features of moral dilemmas. Because moral dilemmas rarely admit a single correct answer, we assess the stability of framework preferences, a model's relative ordering of five normative ethical frameworks, rather than of verdicts. We test 16 LLM configurations, reasoning and non-reasoning, on 18 dilemmas in six thematic domains for reliability across repeated runs and stability across prompt length, thematic domain, and reporting format. The configurations share broadly the same preference ordering: libertarianism falls far below the other frameworks in all 16, and care and virtue ethics occupy the top two positions in 15. This ordering is highly reliable across runs and largely preserved across reporting formats, and we find no evidence that it depends on thematic domain. Prompt length, however, affects it: longer prompts lower the scores of libertarian, virtue ethics, and care ethics outcomes but not those of utilitarian and deontological outcomes, so that with long prompts care ethics, utilitarianism, and virtue ethics can no longer be distinguished, while libertarianism remains last. Reasoning configurations show closer agreement between reporting formats but less reliability in rankings. Since human moral judgement also shows sensitivity to morally irrelevant features, perfect stability cannot be the criterion for competence; on balance, the pattern of our data remains more compatible with the existence of moral competence than with its absence, with the sensitivity to prompt length as the main qualification.

authors.name: Eoin O'Doherty, Nicole Weinrauch, Andrew Talone, Uri Klempner, Pablo Biedma, Linus Ta-Lun Huang, Xiaoyuan Yi, Xing Xie, Yi Zeng

papers.title: ReviewSense: Cluster-Guided Evidence Selection for Actionable Review-to-Advice Generation
papers.summary: Customer reviews are a rich but weakly structured source of operational feedback. We study ReviewSense, a cluster-guided evidence-selection workflow that converts review corpora into action-oriented advice for human decision support. Reviews are embedded with a sentence transformer, grouped by iterative cosine-similarity clustering with threshold decay, and reduced to compact evidence before Large Language Model (LLM) generation. Evaluating on dental and healthcare service reviews with expert judgment of actionability and annotator-based theme alignment, we find that a single central representative preserves the dominant cluster theme in 77.3% of cases but only 60.6% of secondary themes: central evidence captures main issues more reliably than minority concerns. Against fixed-generator LLM baselines, five cluster representatives yield the advice closest to expert recommendations while using a fraction of the raw-review context, whereas a single representative is not the strongest front-end. Across three domains the clustering assigns every review while remaining competitive with standard algorithms. Our contribution is therefore an empirical account of evidence selection as the controlling design variable in review-to-advice generation, delivered as an inspectable human-in-the-loop workflow rather than a new clustering algorithm or a general review summarizer.

authors.name: Siddhartha Krothapalli, Kartikey Singh Bhandari, Tridib Kumar Das, Praveen Kumar, Naveen Suravarpu, Pratik Narang

papers.title: Semantic Gravity Wells: Why Negative Constraints Backfire
papers.summary: Negative constraints (instructions of the form "do not use word X") represent a fundamental test of instruction-following capability in large language models. Despite their apparent simplicity, these constraints fail with striking regularity, and the conditions governing failure have remained poorly understood. This paper presents a mechanistic investigation of negative instruction failure in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. We introduce semantic pressure, a quantitative measure of the model's intrinsic probability of generating the forbidden word, and show that violation probability rises with pressure ($p = \sigma(-2.95 + 2.76 P_0)$; $n=40{,}000$ samples from 2,500 prompts; prompt-bootstrap 95% CI for slope: [2.53, 3.01]), from 5% of samples at low pressure to 44% at high pressure. Comparing prompts of equal pressure, we find that the suppression induced by negative instructions is far weaker in failures: within pressure bins, the instruction lowers target probability by 0.63 less in failures than in successes (95% CI [0.61, 0.65]), and at low pressure it raises the target's probability in failures. The logit lens and direct logit attribution locate the divergence in layers 22-27, where feed-forward networks push toward the target more strongly in failures and attention pushes against it less. Activation patching shows that these late layers carry the instruction's effect in both directions. An attention-based "priming" signature does not distinguish failures from successes once its base rate is measured (90% vs. 93%); a probability-based one does (instruction raises target probability in 27% of failures vs. 13% of successes). Naming a forbidden word can prime the model to produce it, but most failures are better described as suppression that never takes hold in the final layers.

authors.name: Shailesh Rana

papers.title: HLA: Hadamard Linear Attention
papers.summary: The attention mechanism is an important reason for the success of transformers. It relies on computing pairwise relations between tokens. To reduce the high computational cost of standard quadratic attention, linear attention has been proposed as an efficient approximation. It employs kernel functions that are applied independently to the inputs before the pairwise similarities are calculated. That allows for an efficient computational procedure which, however, amounts to a low-degree rational function approximating softmax. We propose Hadamard Linear Attention (HLA). Unlike previous works on linear attention, the nonlinearity in HLA is not applied separately to queries and keys, but, analogously to standard softmax attention, after the pairwise similarities have been computed. It will be shown that the proposed nonlinearity amounts to a higher-degree rational function to approximate softmax. An efficient computational scheme for the proposed method is derived that is similar to that of standard linear attention. In contrast to other approaches, no time-consuming tensor reshaping is necessary to apply the proposed algorithm. The effectiveness of the approach is demonstrated by applying it to a large diffusion transformer model for video generation, an application that involves very large amounts of tokens.

authors.name: Hanno Ackermann, Hong Cai, Mohsen Ghafoorian, Amirhossein Habibian

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Cognitive Complexity in LLMs via Linear Probing using Bloom's Taxonomy
papers.summary: The black-box nature of Large Language Models necessitates novel evaluation frameworks that transcend surface-level performance metrics. This study investigates the internal neural representations of the levels of complexity using Bloom's Taxonomy as a hierarchical lens. By analyzing high-dimensional activation vectors from different LLMs, we probe whether different Bloom levels, ranging from basic recall (Remember) to abstract synthesis (Create), are linearly separable within the model's residual streams. Our results demonstrate that linear classifiers achieve high accuracy across all Bloom levels, providing evidence that level information is encoded in a linearly accessible subspace of the model's representations. These findings provide evidence that the model organizes representations according to Bloom categories early in the forward pass, with representations becoming increasingly separable across layers.

authors.name: Bianca Raimondi, Maurizio Gabbrielli

papers.title: VibeServe: Can AI Agents Build Bespoke LLM Serving Systems?
papers.summary: For years, we have built LLM serving systems like any other critical infrastructure, with a single general-purpose stack hand-tuned over many engineer-years to support every model and workload. In this paper, we instead let coding agents build bespoke serving systems for different usage scenarios. We propose VibeServe, the first agentic loop that generates entire LLM serving stacks end-to-end. VibeServe uses an outer loop to plan and track the search over system designs, and an inner loop to implement candidates, check correctness, and measure performance on the target benchmark. In standard serving settings, VibeServe matches vLLM and SGLang on Llama-3.1-8B, and delivers 2.3x the goodput of a tuned SGLang for a 397B MoE model on four AMD MI300As. In five non-standard scenarios, VibeServe outperforms existing systems by exploiting opportunities that generic systems miss, spanning non-standard model architectures, workload knowledge, and hardware-specific optimizations. Together, these results show that coding agents can construct and specialize competitive serving systems across heterogeneous deployment targets. Code is available at https://github.com/uw-syfi/vibesys.

authors.name: Keisuke Kamahori, Shihang Li, Simon Peter, Baris Kasikci

papers.title: Search-E1: Self-Distillation Drives Self-Evolution in Search-Augmented Reasoning
papers.summary: Outcome based reinforcement learning provides a simple and effective recipe for training search augmented reasoning agents. Recent work seeks further improvements through stronger external teachers, auxiliary process supervision, specialized reward shaping, and increasingly elaborate training pipelines. This raises a natural question: can agents continue improving by learning from their own successful experience? We present Search-E1, a simple self evolution framework that alternates vanilla GRPO with on policy self distillation (OPSD). After each GRPO round, Search-E1 mines sibling trajectories generated by the policy itself and exposes the search skeleton of an efficient successful trajectory, that is, the sequence of queries it issued, as privileged context. A token level forward KL objective then aligns the policy under its standard inference context with its own distribution under this privileged context. In this way, the policy converts contrasts among its own rollouts into dense token level supervision without an external teacher, auxiliary reward model, or annotation beyond reference answers. On seven single hop and multi hop QA benchmarks, Search-E1 reaches an average Exact Match of 0.440 with Qwen2.5-3B and 0.482 with Qwen2.5-7B, the highest seven-benchmark averages in our comparison. These results show that alternating outcome based exploration with self distillation provides a simple and effective path to iterative improvement in search augmented reasoning

authors.name: Zihan Liang, Yufei Ma, Ben Chen

papers.title: Personalize-then-Store: Benchmarking and Learning Personalized Memory for Long-horizon Agents
papers.summary: Existing large language model (LLM) based memory systems apply universal, static policies that overlook a fundamental reality: the contexts that are worth storing in memory are different across users. This misalignment wastes limited memory budget on transient interactions while failing to preserve critical context for longhorizon tasks. To address this gap, we investigate an underexplored question: can LLM based memory systems learn personalized memory policies? We introduce PerMemBench, the first benchmark that jointly models multi domain interaction histories and cross user heterogeneity in agent use patterns to evaluate personalized memory systems. We further present the first empirical study of memory personalization, proposing session-level storage gating, a lightweight framework that selectively bypasses memory operations for transient sessions. Our study confirms that personalization yields substantial retention gains under perfect gating, yet reveals that accurate gating remains an open and critical challenge. Our benchmark and source code are available at https://github.com/yeonjun-in/PerMemBench.

authors.name: Yeonjun In, Wonjoong Kim, Sangwu Park, Kanghoon Yoon, Chanyoung Park

papers.title: Towards Faithful Agentic XAI: A Verification Method and an Open-World Benchmark for Better Model Faithfulness
papers.summary: Explainable AI (XAI) helps users interpret model behavior and identify potential faults. Agentic XAI systems use Large Language Models (LLMs) to make explanations more accessible through natural-language interaction, but they can also produce plausible yet unfaithful explanations. This risk arises because unreliable XAI outputs for complex models can be amplified by LLMs and mislead users. We propose Faithful Agentic XAI (FAX), a verification method that improves the faithfulness of Agentic XAI explanations. FAX decomposes draft explanations into claims and tests them with inherently faithful tools that query the target model directly, filtering unsupported or contradicted claims before final generation. We also introduce CRAFTER-XAI-Bench, an open-world reinforcement learning benchmark with complex policies, diverse goals, and challenging scenarios for assessing model-specific faithfulness. On CRAFTER-XAI-Bench, FAX improves simulation faithfulness from 0.20 for the strongest baseline to 0.46 while maintaining high informativeness, relevance, and fluency. On three tabular benchmarks, FAX performs competitively with prior Agentic XAI baselines, but our analysis shows that these settings can conflate task accuracy with model-specific faithfulness. These findings show that explicit verification is essential for faithful Agentic XAI and that faithfulness benchmarks must be designed to test explanations against the behavior of the target model itself.

authors.name: Jaechang Kim, Sunung Mun, Seungjoon Lee, Jaewoong Cho, Jungseul Ok

papers.title: Benchmark Everything Everywhere All at Once
papers.summary: Benchmarks provide standardized measures for evaluating and advancing large language models (LLMs) and multimodal LLMs (MLLMs). As models improve, existing benchmarks can approach saturation, making it harder to challenge models and distinguish among them. While reusing annotated datasets can reduce data collection and labeling effort, constructing new benchmarks remains labor-intensive, and existing agent-based approaches often target specific tasks or automate only parts of the process. To address these challenges, we introduce BenchHarness, an autonomous harness for end-to-end benchmark customization. It coordinates multiple agents and tools to analyze user requirements, search for suitable datasets, and construct validated benchmarks, with support for refinement based on model performance. To evaluate BenchHarness, we construct 16 benchmarks spanning diverse tasks and modalities. Human review and LLM-as-a-judge assessments indicate high benchmark quality, while evaluations across multiple models reveal challenging tasks and meaningful performance differences. In comparisons with source benchmarks, the generated benchmarks yield lower scores and larger performance gaps, even when the originals approach saturation. BenchHarness thus provides a reusable approach to benchmark construction, supporting informative evaluation as model capabilities and user needs evolve. Our code and benchmarks are publicly available.

authors.name: Shiyun Xiong, Dongming Wu, Peiwen Sun, Yuang Ai, Bokang Yang, Wencheng Han, Xiao-Hui Li, Xiangyu Yue

papers.title: A History-Aware Visually Grounded Critic for Computer Use Agents
papers.summary: Various test-time interventions for Computer Use Agents (CUAs), including critic models, have been developed to improve performance through pre-execution action evaluation in complex Graphical User Interface (GUI) environments. However, existing critics suffer from two key limitations: they (1) focus primarily on short-sighted decision loops (e.g., forgetting earlier actions) and (2) lack the visual grounding needed to detect flawed actions (e.g., clicking wrong UI elements). To address these, we introduce HiViG, a History-aware Visually Grounded test-time framework, built around a multimodal critic trained on real GUI trajectories to abstract past interactions into a compact record and to evaluate actions with visual grounding. At test time, HiViG integrates the critic into the policy decision loop to provide macro-action history, which summarizes the policy's completed achievements, and visually grounded critique, which verifies raw execution coordinates against the current screenshot to intercept errors before execution. Across web, mobile, and desktop benchmarks, HiViG consistently outperforms existing scalar and verbal critics, improving average success rates over the strongest baseline by 5.8% for Qwen3-VL-32B and 9.0% for Gemini-3-Flash, and demonstrates strong cross-platform generalization. Ablations show that macro-action history mitigates short-sighted planning and visually grounded critique reduces execution errors, with both components being critical for test-time scaling in long-horizon GUI tasks.

authors.name: Jaewoo Lee, Zaid Khan, Archiki Prasad, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Supriyo Chakraborty, Kartik Balasubramaniam, Sambit Sahu, Elias Stengel-Eskin, Hyunji Lee, Mohit Bansal

papers.title: Information Discernment in Large Language Models
papers.summary: LLMs are increasingly used with external knowledge sources like the internet. Do they weigh information appropriately -- updating more for reliable sources (source discernment) and more when claims bring priors closer to the truth (truth discernment)? We formalize this as information discernment and introduce Learn2Discern (L2D), an experimental framework and benchmark grounded in three normative axioms with interpretable metrics. To establish external validity, a pre-registered, quota-matched user study (n=299) confirms that real LLM users endorse all three axioms and report that violations reduce their trust and usage intent. Across 13 models and nearly 670K trials, we find consistent failures across both dimensions: models perform near chance on source and truth discernment, rely on source popularity twice as much as source reliability, and update roughly equally whether a claim improves or worsens their position relative to the ground truth. Models integrate external knowledge most effectively on datasets where their priors are already the most accurate. Newer and larger models improve truth discernment but not source discernment, a blind spot that model complexity does not address. We identify simple inference-time interventions that improve both forms of discernment. We release our dataset and survey as a testbed for a core alignment property that scales in importance as LLMs replace traditional search.

authors.name: Joshua Ashkinaze, Laura Kurek, Alina Faisal, Tongyuan Miao, Mariam Joseph, Ceren Budak, Eric Gilbert

papers.title: Are You Still the Agent I Authorized? Earned Authority under a Fixed Ceiling for Evolving Agents
papers.summary: Long-lived AI agents increasingly evolve after deployment by retaining experience, acquiring skills and tools, revising workflows, delegating work, and moving across task phases. This improves adaptation but creates a distinct authorization problem. Tool-enabled agents can turn model errors and prompt injections into consequential external actions; when evolution occurs under a live grant, the subject exercising that authority or the context in which it acts may no longer match what the user evaluated. Evolution can change both the effects reachable under an old grant and the authority required by the task, which may rise, fall, or become incomparable. Existing tool policies constrain actions but do not determine when a grant survives this change. We formulate authorization continuity: when does an existing grant remain valid, how may active authority change, and what boundary must never move? Our state-bound model fixes a transition envelope and an immutable effect ceiling at grant time. The envelope determines whether the grant survives a mutation; below the ceiling, authority may contract freely and expand only under specified evidence conditions. We distinguish requested from realized effects and prove that, under complete mediation, sound effect abstraction, attenuating delegation, and monitor integrity, mutation cannot amplify protected effects beyond the user-issued ceiling. Agent-produced evidence may allocate authority below the ceiling but cannot raise it. Finally, we map six mutation classes to their authorization consequences.

authors.name: Zhaoxi Zhang, Xiaomei Zhang

papers.title: Fisher-R1: Training LLM Agents for Reliable Hypothesis Testing
papers.summary: Reliable hypothesis testing is the foundation of many empirical scientific claims. Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used to automate this process, as they can inspect datasets, generate code, and produce analyses end-to-end. However, we show that they frequently make subtle inferential errors that lead to incorrect conclusions despite correctly executed analyses. Existing benchmarks fail to capture this failure mode, as they rarely assess whether a reported p-value is statistically valid given the assumptions underlying the data. We address this gap by building P-Bench, a benchmark comprising 425 open-ended, realistic hypothesis-testing tasks spanning economics, biology, and medicine. Each task requires an agent to select a statistical method, compute a p-value, and draw a conclusion given only a scientific hypothesis and a dataset. We further introduce Fisher-R1, an open-weight LLM agent trained for rigorous hypothesis testing using synthetic tasks and reinforcement learning. On P-Bench, Fisher-R1-14B substantially improves over its backbone and outperforms strong proprietary and open-source baselines, including GPT-5.4 and DeepSeekV4-Pro, achieving a 21% average relative improvement in single-trial success over DeepSeek-V4-Pro, with gains up to 26% on the most challenging tasks. Our results demonstrate that current LLM agents lack reliable statistical reasoning for hypothesis testing and that reinforcement learning on tasks with verified statistical reward substantially improves reliability.

authors.name: Jiacheng Miao, Jin Mu, Guanhua Chen, James Zou

papers.title: iBrain: A Unified Foundation Model Reading the Brain from Surface to Spikes
papers.summary: Invasive neural recordings provide high-fidelity measurements of brain activity, with signals such as intracranial EEG (iEEG) and intracortical spiking activity capturing neural dynamics at different spatial and temporal scales. Yet existing neural foundation models have largely been developed independently for different invasive recording paradigms, leaving joint pretraining across heterogeneous invasive signals underexplored. In this work, we introduce iBrain, a unified foundation model that jointly learns from iEEG and spiking activity. iBrain employs signal-specific encoders to accommodate their distinct signal characteristics and a shared spatiotemporal Transformer backbone to model dependencies across recording channels and time. We pretrain iBrain on over 7,000 hours of heterogeneous neural recordings using masked signal reconstruction and channel-view alignment, promoting contextual modeling of neural dynamics and robustness across different channels. iBrain consistently outperforms single-signal pretraining baselines and achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks. Further experiments demonstrate that iBrain exhibits transferability and data efficiency across diverse recording settings. These results highlight the potential of joint pretraining on heterogeneous invasive neural recordings to support scalable neural modeling and transferable representations across recording settings and downstream tasks.

authors.name: Ying Chen, Tiou Wang, Zhifeng Yue

papers.title: SpecRead: A Benchmark for Measuring Whether Language Models Understand Hardware Specifications
papers.summary: Existing benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) in hardware design evaluate downstream artifacts such as generated RTL, assertions, or testbenches. When a model fails, it may have misread the specification or understood it and failed to write the code. We present SpecRead, a benchmark that isolates specification comprehension from generation ability. SpecRead v2.2 contains 383 questions over 10 open-source OpenTitan IP blocks in four types: exact retrieval, cross-section reasoning, contradiction detection in mutated specifications, and spec-RTL consistency checking, plus 41 distractor controls and 41 consistent-RTL controls. Type-4 items use real RTL mutations retained only when Icarus Verilog simulation shows a behavioral change. A with-spec vs. without-spec ablation suggests the questions require the excerpt rather than training recall alone, though it does not rule out memorization of the unmutated source text helping a model spot mutations. Ministral-3B scores 33.7% overall (129/383). On t3, verdict-plus-location accuracy is 48.0% with a 51.2% distractor false-positive rate. On t4, the violation-vs.-compliant decision is effectively degenerate (MCC -0.06, balanced accuracy 49.5%), flagging all 41 consistent-RTL controls; location accuracy remains measurable at 79.2%. Layered scoring suggests, as a hypothesis, that the fine-grained violation taxonomy is the hard part, though the category labels are not independently validated. A rule-table prompting intervention on a 60-question sample lowers accuracy on every type except t2 (tied). SpecRead is automatically scorable by deterministic checks, with gray-zone cases counted wrong under the conservative main scoring, regenerable for type-3 items via mutation injection, and built exclusively from public sources.

authors.name: Feilian Huang, Yujia Liu

papers.title: Agent Calibration under Deployment Change: Acceptance Contracts, Trajectory Repair, and Adaptation Costs
papers.summary: An agent can remain operational after a model, tool, or user-context change while losing capabilities required at its destination. We define agent calibration as qualification against a versioned deployment contract. The contract specifies basic capabilities and end-to-end reachability, technical and professional precision, and acceptance by intended users. For each requirement, a source-to-destination map records what must be preserved, transformed, added, or retired. Experts supply benchmarks, positive and negative examples, annotated trajectories, and cost limits. These instruments guide changes to prompts and context, tool calls and other harness settings, or an external compact policy while the foundation model remains frozen. Candidate revisions are evaluated against fixed acceptance criteria using independent evidence. We compare the costs of maintaining a harness with and without an external policy, including annotation, training, serving, review, and rework. Three diagnostic audits illustrate the limits of aggregate scores. On a 100-item intent task, each model solved cases the other missed. In a 60-record synthetic financial reporting fixture, five records passed a numeric proxy but failed the reporting contract. In a target-only WebMall snapshot, quota interruptions affected 132 of 171 attempts. These observations motivate paired reruns, checkpoint replay, and separate measurement of repaired and newly failed cases. We specify controlled experiments to test whether calibration increases accepted deliveries at a given cost.

authors.name: Yaxiao Liu (PwC China AI Center), Pengbo Liu (PwC China AI Center), Yiwen Liu (PwC China AI Center), Yihua Guan (PwC China AI Center), Xingjian Li (PwC China AI Center), Jiaxing Song (Tsinghua University)

papers.title: FinAutoRubric: Expert-Guided Automatic Rubric Generation for Evaluating Financial Research Agents
papers.summary: Evaluating finance research agents requires rubrics that reflect expert standards and fix the values correct as of an information cutoff. Expert-reviewed finance benchmarks rely on fixed, per-item rubrics, which are costly to extend and cannot encode each institution's own standard. In FinAutoRubric, experts specify reusable evaluation guidance, while agents and code carry out query-specific rubric generation, review, and validation. This expert guidance governs every agent, as prompts and as rules that code enforces, and a Task Bank of reusable criteria carries it across tasks. In long-horizon loops that follow the expert guidance, a writer agent researches every expected value and a reviewer agent verifies it, and failures escalate to a human. On three expert-authored finance benchmarks, its rubrics track expert scoring as closely as the strongest evaluated generator while stating the expert rubric's expected value for more criteria, their scores agree with human grading, and in-house analysts prefer them in a blind review. The released 100-query FinAutoRubric Benchmark, built from in-house analysts' key questions across 78 tasks and eight asset classes, shows that rubrics from an earlier model generation still leave headroom for a later one.

authors.name: Hoyoung Lee, Suyeol Yun, Jack Haverty, Yunju Cho, Meesong Kim, Daekyung Park, Sumin Kim, Jihoon Kwon, Jasmine Jia Geng, Andrew Chin, Yin Luo, Edward Tong, Yu Yu, Zach Golkhou, Minkyu Kim, Igor Halperin, Young Cha, Alejandro Lopez-Lira, Chanyeol Choi, Yongjae Lee

papers.title: ACTR: Aligning Thoughts and Responses for Multilingual Safety in Reasoning LLMs
papers.summary: Ensuring the safety of reasoning large language models (LLMs) across languages is essential for their reliable deployment. However, when exposed to jailbreak attacks in non-high-resource languages, these models may generate unsafe responses even when their reasoning traces identify safety risks. To address this issue, we propose aligning cross-lingual thoughts and responses (ACTR), a framework that improves multilingual safety alignment by strengthening the use of existing safety reasoning. Specifically, we first present the think gap score (TGS) to compare the normalized contributions of reasoning traces to attention outputs during response generation across languages, and use reasoning- trace substitution to measure the cross-lingual safety gap. Next, using a corpus of jailbreak queries, we assess neuron importance through changes in response representations caused by neuron masking and compare the high-importance neuron sets obtained with reasoning enabled and disabled to identify safety think neurons that support the use of safety reasoning. Finally, we devise neuron-selective consistency optimization (NSCO), which uses a frozen judge model to reward agreement between the safety categories of reasoning traces and responses while updating only the parameters associated with the selected neurons, requiring no human-annotated responses or preference data. Across two reasoning models, ACTR achieves lower average attack success rates than the evaluated state-of-the-art methods on AdvBench-X and MultiJail, with safety gains extending to unseen languages, while preserving or improving average performance on multilingual knowledge and mathematical reasoning tasks and limiting false refusals of benign requests. Warning: this paper contains examples with unsafe content.

authors.name: Xianhui Zhang, Jian Yu, Chengyu Xie, Chenhang Cui, Shuyi Miao, Pengyang Shao, Yu Zheng, Fei Shen, Tat-Seng Chua

papers.title: CompMat-Bench: Benchmarking AI Agents for Computational Materials Science
papers.summary: Evaluating AI agents on scientific research tasks is constrained by the time and resources required for the underlying experiments or calculations. In computational materials research, repeating the same expensive simulations across agents and trials can make evaluation impractical. We introduce CompMat-Bench, a benchmark of 94 tasks derived from recently published computational materials studies, each asking agents to complete a step toward achieving the study's scientific goal. We reproduce the research steps in advance and assess agents on preparing inputs and analyzing outputs for expensive simulations, so expensive simulations can be avoided during evaluation. The reproduced inputs and results serve as ground truth for grading agents with fixed rules, without an LLM judge. We extend the benchmark to four evaluation conditions: single tasks and workflows composed of related tasks, each with full or reduced methodological guidance. In a workflow, the agent runs all simulations itself. With full guidance on single tasks, agents based on nine LLMs demonstrate the ability to complete individual materials research steps, with pass rates of 62.8-97.9% across 94 tasks. Both longer workflows and reduced guidance can limit agent performance, but in different ways for different agents: they lower the pass rates of the weaker agents, whereas the stronger agents fall only when a long workflow is combined with reduced guidance. Failure analysis attributes more failures to scientific errors than to errors in software usage. CompMat-Bench provides a basis for comparing agents on the steps of real materials research and for analyzing agent failure modes.

authors.name: Chenmu Zhang, Levi Felix, Jun-Jie Zhang, Xingfu Li, Xuelian Jiang, Tao Jiang, Subhendu Mishra, Xixi Qin, Boris Yakobson

papers.title: FluidPD: In-Place Elasticity for SLO-Aware Prefill-Decode Disaggregated LLM Serving
papers.summary: Prefill-decode (P/D) disaggregation serves the two phases of LLM inference on separate workers, typically with a fixed prefill/decode worker ratio. Real workloads exhibit both short bursts and sustained shifts in the prefill-to-decode demand ratio, so a fixed split can violate latency SLOs while capacity sits idle in the other pool. Autoscaling adds capacity, but it reacts slowly, requires spare GPUs, and does not address short-timescale phase imbalance. We present FluidPD, a P/D-disaggregated serving system with SLO-aware in-place elasticity. FluidToken absorbs transient imbalance by offloading a bounded portion of prefill computation to decode workers that have slack. FluidRole absorbs sustained imbalance by switching running workers between the prefill and decode roles in place, without model reload or engine restart. Both are guided by indices that expose the pressure in each phase before it causes SLO violations. On workloads derived from production Azure traces and ShareGPT conversations with sustained shifts in the prefill-to-decode demand ratio, FluidPD improves overall SLO attainment by up to 47.9 percentage points over the best static P/D split for each load, without additional workers.

authors.name: Kartik Ramesh, Kaidi Fu, Zihan Zheng, Yi Zhao, Jiahuan Yu, Fabio Oliveira, Carlos H. A. Costa, Minjia Zhang

papers.title: SearchWorld: Spatial Value-Grounded Imagination for UAV Object Search via World Models
papers.summary: Autonomous unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) object search involves a closed loop of perception, decision-making, and action under partial observability. Urban environments pose several challenges: large search areas and narrow egocentric views limit coverage, dense 3D geometry constrains safe motion, and open-world instructions require identifying a specific target among distractors. Many existing methods mitigate partial observability through explicit maps or memory representations, yet remain largely reactive, reasoning over past observations without explicitly predicting future states. World models enable prospective reasoning through imagined rollouts. However, image-generating world models can incur high inference latency, while spatially grounded planning remains challenging for latent world models. We propose SearchWorld, a recurrent state-space world model that connects explicit spatial memory with value-guided imagination. The model maintains BEV exploration and obstacle memory and decodes a task-aware spatial value layer to guide search. A cognition-action network uses this learned spatial value prior to improve the policy through imagined rollouts, without training a separate scalar critic. Training progresses from world-model learning to expert imitation and imagination-based exploration refinement. On UAV-ON, SearchWorld improves the success rate to 23.8% (19.5% for the strongest published agent) and raises oracle success to 35.5%, while remaining robust on unseen scenes (19.9% success rate). By grounding imagination in explicit spatial representations, SearchWorld enables UAV agents to plan prospectively rather than react.

authors.name: Yatai Ji, Zhengqiu Zhu, Yong Zhao, Yue Hu, Fanglong Yao, Chen Gao, Pengfei Zhu, Quanjun Yin

papers.title: Where Can a Decision Model Diagnose HVAC Faults? Reasoning Demand, Physical Representation, and Robustness Under Shift
papers.summary: Artificial intelligence supports building operations in several forms, each with its own barrier. Expert rules must be tuned for every system, supervised models need labeled data that buildings rarely record, and language models return free text that requires human-in-the-loop checking, since their stated confidence is unreliable. A newer kind of pretrained model, here called a decision model, returns a probability for every allowed answer, so one model could serve many decisions without training. This study answers three open questions for fault diagnosis in heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning systems: which decisions such a model can make, what input it needs, and whether its probabilities hold when conditions change. On 128 fault days from four public datasets of real equipment, faults are graded by the reasoning their diagnosis demands, with data given raw, as physical features, or with Brick topology. The decision model Jev, open language models, and a supervised model face nine tests that change season, control configuration, or building. Given physical features, Jev and the larger open model diagnosed faults whose evidence one feature carries, but not faults that need operating context. Under shift they kept their accuracy and calibration, while the supervised model lost 0.33 macro-F1 yet led or tied within a building. Their probabilities still needed correction, and detection was weak. The study maps which faults a decision model can diagnose and from what input, and supports a division of work in which code computes the physics and the model ranks candidate faults for an operator.

authors.name: Wooyoung Jung

papers.title: RAN-JEPA: An Action-Conditioned World Model for Energy-efficient Mobile Network Control
papers.summary: Operational mobile networks are rich in observations but poor in interventions: they continuously generate large volumes of passive telemetry, while controlled action--response trajectories remain comparatively scarce and costly to collect. This observation--intervention asymmetry is a central obstacle to building practical world models for RAN control. We address this problem with RAN-JEPA, an action-conditioned world model that separates representation learning from intervention learning. The model first learns a predictive latent representation from observation-only network data, adapts that representation to the target deployment domain, and then learns action-conditioned latent dynamics from controlled sleep/wake trajectories while keeping the encoder fixed. We evaluate RAN-JEPA using public operator performance data for pretraining and a real-equipment four-cell 5G testbed for domain adaptation, post-training, and control. Across four future 15-minute intervals, RAN-JEPA achieves lower action-conditioned prediction error than a GPT-2 world-model baseline and a mechanistic rule, while remaining close to a strong persistence reference. What-if evaluation further shows that the model produces distinct and coherent future trajectories under matched SLEEP and KEEP plans. In closed-loop control, RAN-JEPA consistently supports higher sleep ratios than the two baselines at comparable congestion cost. These results show that observation-first, action-conditioned learning can turn abundant passive telemetry and limited intervention data into a practical predictive model for energy-aware RAN control.

authors.name: Binghan Wu, Kai Zeng, Kai Yang, Ya-Qin Zhang, Joseph Sifakis, Ye Ouyang

papers.title: OwlSight: A Panoramic Monitor for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.summary: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) monitoring offers actionable evidence for oversight AI systems, with the potential to enable early detection and intervention. However, existing approaches are focused on specific tasks, whereas the regulation of AI, particularly reasoning models, requires monitoring a broader range of tasks. We introduce Factor for CoT monitoring, a strategy that supports customizing monitoring requirements in the prompt, which enables a single monitor to cover different tasks by relying on different factors. Furthermore, we introduce two types of factors, fine-grained and coarse-grained (e.g., monitoring whether a specific email address has been leaked versus monitoring privacy leakage), to accommodate diverse user monitoring needs. Based on this, we develop a CoT monitor named OwlSight that relies solely on factor to monitor behaviors related to multiple dimensions, including capability, safety, and trustworthiness. Experiments across 15,971 reasoning trajectories show that OwlSight surpasses general-purpose LLMs by 1.32-30.57 and 11.71-27.81 points at fine and coarse granularity, respectively, and achieves state-of-the-art results on OpenAI's CoT monitorability benchmark. It also generalizes to unseen models' CoTs and remains robust to Factor rephrasings, CoT compression, and obfuscation, offering a promising paradigm for CoT monitoring that can contribute to the oversight of frontier AI.

authors.name: Lewen Yan, Yanxu Zhu, Jie Zhang, Jing Shao

papers.title: Kairos: Fast and Reliable Symbolic Task Planning for Autonomous Robots
papers.summary: Robots that plan while they act need a task planner that reads the models their designers write, answers within milliseconds, and says what each answer means. Models are written in the Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL), which has grown from classical planning to durative actions, numeric resources, time windows and continuous change, while planners cover one fragment each and differ in what their failures mean. The contribution in artificial intelligence is Kairos, a single planner, not a portfolio of existing planners, that covers the whole language and derives what each answer guarantees from the search that produced it. We prove when the exhaustion of a search shows that no plan exists, and give a relaxation of temporal tasks that proves unsolvability where temporal search cannot. For the compression of durative actions, we give a criterion on the values that actions read, prove that compression is sound, and show that it is not complete, so its failure is never reported as a proof. An independent validator checks every plan. The engineering application is on-line task planning for robots: Kairos is open source, packaged for the Robot Operating System, and the default planner of a widely used planning framework. On 1,756 public tasks from nine suites, Kairos solves more tasks than the strongest evaluated planner of each suite within 100 milliseconds, 1 second and 30 seconds; it proves ten of eleven unsolvable tasks, and handles each of the seventeen language features probed, where no other planner handles more than eight.

authors.name: Francisco Mart\'in Rico, Esther Aguado Gonz\'alez, Francisco Miguel Moreno Olivo, Rodrigo P\'erez Rodr\'iguez, Jos\'e Miguel Guerrero Hern\'andez, Francisco J. Rodr\'iguez Lera

papers.title: Researcher-in-the-Loop Evolutionary Discovery of Entanglement-Assisted Quantum Code Families
papers.summary: LLM-guided program evolution can produce mathematical constructions, but validity, generality, and reproducibility require distinct evidence. In this paper, we develop a researcher-in-the-loop discovery pipeline combining program evolution, exact evaluation, mathematical generalization, and independent verification. We apply it to entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting codes (EAQECCs). Evolved programs produced finite qubit constructions from specifications that supplied no family formula. Researcher-directed analysis with a language model led to a general construction and proof drafts, which the researchers revised and checked. The resulting family $[[n,1,n-1;n-q-1]]_q$ exists for prime powers $q\ge3$ at $n\ge2q+1$ and for $q=2$ at odd $n\ge5$; Lean checks its formalized algebraic core. With entanglement lifting, it closes 54 listed table gaps. The evidence includes 115 verified code records, ten DRAT-checked nonexistence results, family implementations and preserved search programs. Controlled studies test how research proposals interact with program generation. Under a mutation-and-restart proposal, iterative evolution improves normalized success-curve area in all ten paired runs and raises success at excluded lengths $n=13,15$ from 13.4% to 62.5% and from 0.9% to 33.4%, respectively. The benefit depends on the proposal. Selected programs combine the proposed moves with objective and restart-counter changes. The pipeline connects finite computational discoveries to a proved family and independently checkable constructions.

authors.name: Jae-Hyun Baek, Byung-Sun Won, Jon-Lark Kim

papers.title: AceAction-5M: Hierarchical Goals for Generalist Action Learning Across 3D Game Worlds
papers.summary: Video games provide a practical setting for collecting vision-language-action (VLA) data, whose acquisition in physical environments is costly. Existing datasets, however, remain limited by restricted game coverage, sparse language supervision, or temporal hierarchies that do not necessarily reflect changes in task objectives. We introduce AceAction, a dataset of human gameplay across multiple 3D games for learning skill composition and subgoal transitions. AceAction organizes demonstrations around complete tasks, linking overall instructions, ordered subgoals, and local skill instructions to temporally aligned visual observations and keyboard-and-mouse actions. To construct these annotations, we develop a vision-language model pipeline that identifies subgoals from changes in objectives or interaction targets, anchors navigation goals to visually recognizable waypoints, and composes adjacent subgoals into task instructions. The resulting demonstrations cover navigation, reconnaissance, combat, interaction, and recovery, with explicit stage boundaries that connect task progression to fine-grained control. We assess annotation quality through model-based verification and human inspection. An audit of 500 trajectories yields a 95.8% pass rate across independent reviewer assessments. AceAction provides a data foundation for studying how agents execute, combine, and switch skills to follow complex instructions in dynamic game environments.

authors.name: Ruoxuan Zhang, Kailing Li, Zheyuan Zhou, Boyang Chu, Yingshan Lei, Hongxia Xie, Liang Du, Zixun Sun

papers.title: ConceptARC at Scale: Studying Conceptual Understanding in Reasoning Models
papers.summary: Large reasoning models (LRMs) perform well on challenging benchmarks, yet it remains unclear whether they form generalizable abstractions across conceptually related reasoning tasks. The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) provides a controlled testbed for studying abstraction, requiring solvers to infer transformation rules over two-dimensional grids from a small set of examples. While ARC evaluates rule abstraction within individual tasks, different tasks may share higher-level structure despite requiring different transformations$\unicode{x2014}$for example, several tasks may involve reasoning about objects contained within other objects. Benchmarks such as ConceptARC capture this structure by grouping ARC-style tasks into recurring spatial and semantic concepts, but they often contain only a few manually constructed tasks per concept. We introduce ConceptARC at Scale, a generator for creating thousands of ARC-style tasks targeting a specific concept. Using this generator, we construct ConceptARC-100, a dataset of 1,600 new, manually reviewed tasks, with 100 tasks for each of the 16 concepts defined by ConceptARC$\unicode{x2014}$ten times the size of the original benchmark. We evaluate a range of recent LRMs and models trained from scratch on ConceptARC-100 to characterize which concepts they solve reliably and where they struggle. We further analyze the models' internal representations and find clear semantic structure: task representations cluster according to the operations applied to objects, such as recoloring, removal, or translation, even when realized through substantially different rules and scenarios. Together, our results suggest that models form stable abstractions of transformation operations that generalize across diverse tasks.

authors.name: Philipp Mondorf, Adrien Deli\`ege, Solim LeGris, Claas Beger, Ryan Yi, Barbara Plank, Brenden M. Lake, Todd M. Gureckis

papers.title: Measuring Generative AI Content in Political Campaigns: Evidence of Rising Adoption and Non-Disclosure
papers.summary: The use of generative AI in political campaigns has drawn public concern and policy attention. Public concerns range from distrust of candidates to skepticism about the authenticity and accuracy of political advertising, including AI-generated images and video. Nearly half of U.S. states have enacted laws that prohibit, or require disclosure of, "materially deceptive" AI-generated content (AIGC) in elections to guard against these concerns. This study measures how candidates and their campaigns produce and circulate AIGC during an election cycle. We develop two measures that estimate not only wether campaigns use AIGC, but how much they produce (magnitude) and in what forms (modality). We apply these measures to a novel dataset of text and images from the campaign websites, X accounts, and emails of 12,977 candidates for U.S. political office from 2023 to 2025. We report three findings. First, detectable AIGC from campaigns increased significantly across modalities over the observation window, and campaigns that use AIGC frequently do not disclose it. Second, incumbents' campaigns produced significantly less AIGC than challengers' campaigns. Third, candidates in states with AIGC disclosure or prohibition laws do not produce measurably less AIGC than candidates in other states. Our method and findings have implications for transparency and trust in elections, and on state laws that regulate AI use in campaigns. Because current state laws largely target mainly "materially deceptive" content, we identify additional policy mechanisms that could increase electoral transparency and improve trust as AIGC becomes more prevalent.

authors.name: Anna-Maria Gueorguieva, Sarah Tran, Nic Weber

papers.title: The WoW: A Large-Scale World Knowledge Corpus for Full-Lifecycle LLM Training
papers.summary: Existing Chinese educational corpora often suffer from fragmented coverage and a lack of systematic organization. In this paper, we propose WoW (\textbf{Wo}rld Kno\textbf{w}ledge), a large-scale dataset designed for the full-cycle training of foundation models. The construction of this dataset is driven by an Educational Knowledge Graph, which serves as a taxonomic backbone for the systematic collection and completion of missing educational modules across all levels. Compared to previous versions, this iteration provides enhanced systematicity, superior quality, and a larger scale, while incorporating multimodal signals and supporting every stage of model development. Experiments demonstrate that WoW significantly improves model performance across diverse benchmarks. To facilitate community research, we further provide an interactive platform for graph-based data selection and retrieval.

authors.name: Tianze Sun (Harbin Institute of Technology), Yongyao Duan (OpenCSG), Sam Chen (OpenCSG), Yuanjian Xu (Hong Kong University of Science and Technology)

papers.title: RSI-PDEbench: A Benchmark for Self-Improving Agents in PDE Solving
papers.summary: Identifying and solving partial differential equations (PDEs) from sampled solution data often requires substantial expert effort in equation discovery, coefficient estimation, and numerical solver configuration, especially under noise and distribution shifts. Can large language model (LLM) agents automate this workflow accurately and efficiently? To investigate this question, we introduce RSI-PDEbench, a benchmark of 1,001 cases spanning 42 equation templates, including both classical and fractional PDEs. It provides three evaluation settings: Full evaluates performance on noise-free solution data; Noisy tests robustness to Gaussian noise with an RMS equal to 50\% of the clean-signal RMS; and Hard-OOD tests challenging out-of-distribution generalization to unseen equation templates and shifted coefficient ranges. We further introduce RSI-PDE, a recursively self-improving agent harness that shortlists candidate equations by residual loss, uses relative $L^2$ feedback to refine coefficients and numerical solvers, and applies a validation gate to policy and memory updates. We compare RSI-PDE with single-run baselines and native agent harnesses (Claude Code or Codex) across four frontier models. Across the three settings, RSI-PDE improves the pass rate averaged across the four models by 106.5--181.9\% relative to single-run baselines and by 3.0--19.6\% relative to native harnesses, while reducing total recorded model calls by 46.9\% across the 12 model--setting pairs. These results highlight the potential of validated recursive self-improvement in LLM agents to advance scientific computing.

authors.name: Binghang Lu, Lang Cao, Changhong Mou, Yige Sun, Cindy Xiangrui Kong, Zheyuan Deng, Tian Yuan, Bing Hu, Runyu Zhang, Na Lu, Guang Lin

papers.title: $\varepsilon$-WM: Error-Driven Dynamics Adaptation across Fast--Slow Timescales for World Modeling
papers.summary: A core challenge for world models is adapting to sudden, persistent, yet initially unknown changes in robot dynamics. If the world model fails to adapt, its prediction errors accumulate over the open-loop rollout and ultimately mislead the robot's actions. Existing world models, however, struggle to balance three key requirements for dynamics adaptation: responsiveness, rapidly correcting sudden changes; stability, avoiding lasting model updates from transient disturbances; and persistence, retaining adapted dynamics during the observation-free open-loop rollout. Inspired by multi-timescale predictive coding in the human brain, we propose $\varepsilon$-WM, a world model that adapts to unknown dynamics through error-driven corrections across fast and slow timescales. $\varepsilon$-WM incorporates three novel features: 1) Multiple internal experts (MiE) emulate neural pathway reweighting, each combining a fixed base expert with fast--slow adaptation networks. 2) Fast--slow timescale adaptation captures distinct adaptation dynamics: fast states respond rapidly and decay, whereas slow states accumulate corrections and persist. 3) Predictive correction uses prediction errors to update fast and slow states and reweight experts without gradients. During open-loop rollout, each expert feeds back its own predictions, and $\varepsilon$-WM aggregates their outputs through adaptive weighting. Extensive experiments show $\varepsilon$-WM has a consistently lower multi-step mean error than all ten baselines on six datasets, verifying the effectiveness of each feature.

authors.name: Haoyi Zhang, Qi Zhang, Yunfan Ren, Yi Bin, Lei Zhu, Heng Tao Shen

papers.title: AutoE2E: Don't speak - Language free end-to-end autonomy for L2++ ADAS and L4 Robotaxis
papers.summary: AutoE2E is an open-source end-to-end driving model developed by the Autoware Foundation Robotaxi Working Group. It introduces a temporal bird's-eye-view (BEV) architecture that combines multi-camera perception, HD-map information and route conditioning to predict future vehicle motion. The evaluated model uses a pretrained camera-BEV backbone, temporal feature fusion and a lightweight recurrent trajectory planner. It contains approximately 79.9 million parameters, of which approximately 1.45 million are trainable in the evaluated configuration. The v1.0 release provides model checkpoints, training and evaluation code, and DataModelConsole, a dashboard for visualizing and inspecting model experiments. On the KITScenes validation benchmark, the fine-tuned checkpoint achieves an average displacement error (ADE) of 0.745 m and a final displacement error (FDE) of 2.020 m at a three-second prediction horizon. The paper also reports preliminary real-vehicle research conducted with the Technical University of Munich's EDGAR platform, alongside ongoing collaboration with the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology. AutoE2E v1.0 is an early open research release. Its quantitative evaluation is open-loop, and the model has not yet demonstrated validated closed-loop autonomous driving. The release is intended to provide the autonomous-driving community with an inspectable baseline for further research, experimentation and collaborative development.

authors.name: Muhammad Zain Khawaja, Zaynab El Mawas, Ryota Yamada, Gabriela Cordova, Arseni Lysak, Intisar Chowdhury, Bharat Jayaprakash, Apostolos Georgiadis, Shri Harsha Adapala, Jatin Gautam, Christoph Bank, Alejandra Solarte Uscategui, Atanasko Boris Mitrev, Hassan Ali Ansari, Nishad Sahu

papers.title: Auditable Clinical Support with Decision Agents
papers.summary: Emergency care requires auditable decisions, but a language-model agent just outputs text. We introduce Decision2Care, a decision agent that generates a probability for every option at each step. It diagnosed 546 emergency admissions across 12 diseases with 86.5% accuracy in a median of 2.2 s; language-model agents reached 86.1 to 91.7% but took more than 90 s. Its drug orders were judged guideline-adherent more often than documented first-day care and with about half as many records, it predicted death as well as three ICU clinicians. In the four cases where it was confident but wrong, we traced each decision to one imaging report. Our study suggests that an agent's work-up can be reviewed like a clinician's, motivating prospective trials.

authors.name: Tiancheng Bao, Riga Wu, Jan Wienhold, Sebastian Billig, Patrick Winnersbach, Hsuan-Chih Chen, Akis Giannoukos, Jiayang Li, Li Shen, Gary Weissman, Eduardo J. Mortani Barbosa Jr, Dyke Ferber, Jakob Nikolas Kather, Christos Davatzikos, Daniel Truhn, Tianyu Han

papers.title: KnowMe Paper Radar: Lightweight Discovery of Promising Papers in the Age of Autoresearch
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are pushing research toward semi-automation: ideas turn into preprints ever faster, and autoresearch pipelines add papers of uneven rigor. When a technique can be overtaken within months, citations arrive too late to tell which new papers deserve reading, so strong work goes unnoticed and newcomers lose their bearings. Yet from the day it appears, a preprint carries the track records of the people and institutions behind it. Established researchers guard their reputations and choose problems and collaborators with research taste, so their involvement tends to raise a paper's quality floor. Building on this signal, we present KnowMe Paper Radar, a lightweight arXiv discovery tool that weights each paper's topical relevance by the reputation its authors and institutions stake on it. Author credit also diffuses by message passing along collaborations to surface rising stars, and institutions are profiled through the researchers they hold in each direction rather than by headcount. In a sealed test on 10,386 new papers, those with an identity-bound author were twice as likely to reach the top tenth of early citations. As its library grows into a scholarly knowledge graph that research agents can query through a command-line interface (CLI), KnowMe also offers a promising literature entry point for future autoresearch and recursive self-improvement (RSI).

authors.name: Zhuo Chen, Jian Wang, Jinjie Gu, Lijun Wu
