papers.title: MuSTRNG: A Muon-Based Synchronizable True Random Number Generation System
papers.summary: Cosmic-ray muons provide naturally occurring stochastic events detectable by spatially separated devices, offering a potential physical source for synchronized random-bit generation. This is possible because the same physical muons can be independently detected by both devices and used to derive corresponding random-bit segments. Therefore, identifying common muon events and correctly aligning the event sequences are essential for synchronized random-bit generation. This article presents MuSTRNG, a muon-based synchronizable true random number generation system with two synchronization methods: Tracking--Tracking and Tracking--Nontracking. For Tracking--Tracking synchronization, track-based screening removes events whose reconstructed tracks do not intersect the detector area of the other device; angle-based screening partitions reconstructed directions into angular bins and aligns the event sequences to remove inconsistent pairs; and timestamp-based screening compares higher-order timestamp bits to further suppress residual mismatches. Tracking--Nontracking synchronization applies track-based screening only at the tracking-capable device, followed by timestamp-based screening between the two devices. A prototype with two tracking-capable devices was evaluated. For Tracking--Tracking synchronization, the three-stage process reduced the invalid-event ratio to 0.28% using 15-bit random segments, while the generated bit sequences showed generally favorable results in the applicable NIST SP~800-22 tests. Reprocessing the data without track information from one device provided preliminary support for Tracking--Nontracking synchronization, yielding an invalid-event ratio of 0.30% using 5-bit random segments. These results demonstrate the feasibility of muon-based synchronized random-bit generation under different device configurations, with potential application to secure communications.

authors.name: Bohang Zou, Shubin Liu, Yu Wang, Ting Wang, Changqing Feng, Zhongtao Shen

papers.title: Skysail: Altitude Control of Long-Duration Weather Balloons by Extracting Work from Wind Shear
papers.summary: Long-duration weather balloons collect repeated atmospheric profiles by venting lifting gas and dropping ballast, but these finite consumables limit the number of profiles each balloon can obtain. We present an altitude-control system that extracts mechanical work from atmospheric wind shear. A small wing suspended 450 m below a zero-pressure balloon experiences relative airflow from the wind velocity difference between the two altitudes. Controlling the wing's pitch produces aerodynamic forces that drive ascent and descent. We develop a model for sizing the system, a lightweight aerodynamic governor for tether deployment, and a control architecture for altitude holding and repeated profiling. Flight experiments conducted over two years accurate control of vertical motion. During a 43-hour interval, the system completed eleven profiles and accumulated 53 km of vertical travel without releasing ballast or venting gas. A separate eight-day flight completed 24 profiles exceeding 1 km in vertical extent, accumulating 159 km of vertical travel. Control authority depends on the available wind shear, with conventional ballast and vent actuation retained for trim and fallback control. These results demonstrate that atmospheric wind shear can sustain repeated balloon profiling while reducing dependence on consumable actuators.

authors.name: Michal Adamkiewicz, Andrey Sushko

papers.title: TyxonQ: A Workflow Layer for Quantum Computing in Chemistry
papers.summary: Quantum computational chemistry is often framed around a hybrid quantum solver. In practical applications, however, bottlenecks to adoption also lie in the surrounding multiscale workflow. A molecular problem may combine classical molecular mechanics and dynamics, conventional electronic-structure calculations, and a quantum solver for selected orbitals or embedded fragments. This division of work is particularly relevant when a chemically important electronic subspace is strongly correlated. The size of the electronic Hilbert space and the qubit, noise, and circuit-depth constraints of noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices make active-space and embedding choices central to a feasible quantum calculation. The resulting energies and gradients must remain consistent with the surrounding classical simulation. We present TyxonQ, a workflow layer that connects these levels of treatment rather than addressing only the hybrid quantum algorithm. Four integration interfaces link PySCF-compatible energy/force scanners and embedding, solver adapters, simulator and hardware backends, and classical consumers. The implementation combines QM/MM and fragment embedding with conventional CCSD/FCI fragment solvers, variational and sampling-based quantum methods, and adapters for ASE, i-PI, OpenMM, LAMMPS (through i-PI), and MDI. We describe the contracts and audit coverage, and evaluate correctness, switching cost, reproducibility, and artifact portability on small chemistry workflows, distinguishing executed paths from source-level support. The purpose of TyxonQ is to support incremental integration of quantum calculations into existing computational chemistry workflows, including those used in industry, while retaining appropriate classical treatments elsewhere.

authors.name: Xiaoran Li, Zhi Yin, Zhupeng Han, Zhengquan Pan, Kangyu Zheng

papers.title: Ion and electron temperature recovery for Irkutsk incoherent scatter measurements
papers.summary: Recovering ion and electron plasma temperatures from Irkutsk Incoherent Scatter Radar (IISR) data is a challenge due to rapid Faraday rotation, which significantly distorts signal correlation profiles. This paper presents an adaptation of the full-profile analysis (FPA) method tailored to the specific conditions of the IISR using a two-step inverse problem framework. The core novelty of the approach lies in the integration of data from both narrowband and wideband channels: experimental power profiles from the wideband channel are incorporated directly into the forward model for temperature recovery. By mathematically establishing the link between the wideband signal amplitude and the temperature ratio, we introduce a non-linear constraint that significantly narrows the solution search space. This addresses the problem of "stretched" global minima in the objective functional, effectively filtering out physically inconsistent results. The inverse problem is solved using the Improved Stochastic Ranking Evolution Strategy (ISRES), which enables fully automated parameter estimation without the need for manual initial guesses.

authors.name: V. P. Tashlykov, A. V. Medvedev, V. P. Lebedev, I. V. Kichigin

papers.title: Estimating subcritical multiplication from stochastic neutron noise: a branching Brownian motion model for leakage counts
papers.summary: A neutron detector placed outside a subcritical system records fission chains as correlated bursts of counts. The time dependence of these correlations gives access to the $\alpha$ eigenvalues governing the decay of the system and, with additional physical information, to its effective multiplication factor $k_{\mathrm{eff}}$. The usual analysis relies on point kinetics, which ignores where chains are born and which neutrons escape. We examine this approximation in a model simple enough to be solved: branching Brownian motion, that is, one-group neutron diffusion with capture and fission, in a domain whose absorbing boundary plays the role of the detector. For a stationary Poisson source we derive the Feynman $Y$ function (the count variance-to-mean ratio minus one) by following pairs of neutrons from their common ancestor to their detection. In a homogeneous cube the result is an explicit sum over spatial modes whose weights are fixed by the geometry and the source. We compare it with direct branching simulations and with one-speed OpenMC transport calculations in which fission is sampled with analog reaction selection and FREYA multiplicities. At the longest simulated gate the model agrees with transport to about $1\%$ at $k=0.8$ and $0.9$, and to $10\%$ at $k=0.5$. The corresponding point-model discrepancies range from $25$ to $48\%$. When geometry, source and material parameters are known, retaining the spatial modes also reduces the bias on the inferred multiplication factor. Two extensions prepare the use of the model in inverse problems. Correlations between opposite faces distinguish systems that share the same fundamental decay rate but differ in leakage, and a hierarchy of three stationary problems links this spatial benchmark to multiplicity counting. Modal convergence, detector imbalance and spectral evolution remain limitations for quantitative inference.

authors.name: Antoine Bessemoulin, Eric Dumonteil

papers.title: Monte Carlo-based secondary dose check platform for the world's first ultra-compact upright proton therapy system
papers.summary: Objective. This work aimed to develop and validate an independent Monte Carlo (MC) secondary dose check of the RayStation treatment planning system (TPS) for the Mevion S250-FIT, the world's first ultra-compact upright proton therapy system. Approach. The treatment nozzle, including the energy modulation system of boron carbide and polycarbonate plates and the adaptive aperture, was modeled in the TOPAS (TOol for PArticle Simulation) MC code, and the beam model was commissioned against integrated depth dose curves, in-air spot profiles, and dose per monitor unit measured at 12 energy settings. Based on this model, an in-house converter, RayStation2TOPAS, recalculates the TPS plans by reconstructing each pencil beam spot, the aperture for each energy layer, and the seated patient's rotation. In total, 15 water phantom plans and 25 clinical plans were recalculated and compared with the TPS by the point dose, with a tolerance of 5%, and by three-dimensional gamma analysis at 3%/2mm, with a pass rate of at least 90%. Main results. The simulated proton range agreed with the measurement within 0.25mm, the spot full width at half maximum within 6.8%, and the dose per monitor unit within 1.3%. The point dose differed from the TPS by -0.76% to +1.98% in the water phantom plans and by -3.03% to +3.99% in the clinical plans, with gamma pass rates of 96.39% to 99.93% and 90.08% to 99.98%, so every plan passed both tests. Significance. To our knowledge, this is the first independent MC secondary dose check for the S250-FIT, and it complements measurement-based patient-specific quality assurance of its plans.

authors.name: Toghrul Alakbarzade, Emir Musa Olgun, Yuan James Rao, Billy W Loo Jr, Adam Johansson, Yong Yang, Murat Surucu, Mehmet Burcin Unlu, Serdar Charyyev

papers.title: Transport Layer-Driven Optimization of Color and Efficiency in TADF OLEDs for Large-Area Applications
papers.summary: Balancing structural simplicity with high efficiency is crucial for practical applications of organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs), especially in large-area lighting devices. Optimizing the charge-transport layers in multilayer OLEDs controls the recombination zone within the emissive layer, thereby enhancing the device's performance. Herein, we experimentally and computationally investigate how the thicknesses of the electron and hole transport layers affect the performance of orange-red thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) OLEDs. Using a TADF emitter, 2-[4-(diphenylamino)phenyl]-10,10-dioxide-9H-thioxanthen-9-one (TXO-TPA), at 10 wt\% concentration in 4,4-Bis(N-carbazolyl)-1,1-biphenyl (CBP) host, we achieve a maximum external quantum efficiency ($\eta_{EQE}$) of 20.86\% and a peak luminance of 32,800 cd m$^{-2}$. Using a combination of drift-diffusion and optical simulations, we reveal how variations in hole- and electron-transport-layer thicknesses modulate the charge-carrier balance and shift the recombination zone within the emissive layer. This tuning not only optimizes exciton formation but also enables color tuning from green to red without altering the emissive material. Our findings highlight the critical role of transport layer engineering in achieving efficient, color-controlled OLEDs with simplified architectures. Furthermore, we successfully demonstrate a large-area OLED device (~20 cm$^{2}$), achieving an impressive $\eta_{EQE}$ of 17\%, underscoring the scalability and practicality of our approach for general lighting applications.

authors.name: Manish Kumar, Jawid Nikan, Luiz Pereira

papers.title: Energy cascade spectrum in wave turbulence of a two-dimensional quantum fluid
papers.summary: In the two-dimensional (2D) Gross-Pitaevskii model for a Bose gas, the naive dimensional non-equilibrium wave-turbulence power-law prediction for the direct energy cascade coincides with thermal equilibrium and therefore carries no energy flux. We resolve this degeneracy by deriving a logarithmically corrected spectrum that supports a positive, constant energy flux toward small scales. A systematic asymptotic expansion of the wave-kinetic collision integral determines the logarithmic exponent to be 1/3, while the small-scale dissipation scale sets the upper cutoff in the logarithmic correction. Regularization of a marginal infrared divergence at the forcing scale yields an estimate of the spectral prefactor for asymptotically well-separated forcing and dissipation scales. Simulations of the Gross-Pitaevskii and wave-kinetic equations support the predicted spectral shape. Over finite spectral ranges, the correction produces apparent power laws steeper than the dimensional prediction, offering a possible explanation for the steep spectra observed in 2D Bose gas experiments. Our approach provides a systematic framework for constructing wave turbulent cascade spectra when the power-law prediction is degenerate with thermodynamic equilibrium.

authors.name: Ying Zhu, Jason Laurie, Giorgio Krstulovic, Sergey Nazarenko

papers.title: Ferroionic CuCrP2S6 Integrated Silicon Photonics for Neuromorphic Computing
papers.summary: Neuromorphic photonic computing calls for optical states that combine stimulus accumulation, spontaneous relaxation, and nonvolatile state retention without continuous power dissipation. Here, we demonstrate a ferroionic photonic platform by integrating layered van der Waals CuCrP2S6 onto silicon microring resonators using a back-end integration process. Electrical pulsing produces unidirectional blue shifts in the optical resonance, consistent with field-driven redistribution of mobile Cu ions and giving rise to a history-dependent optical response. The resulting optical state is strongly pulse dependent, exhibiting both volatile and nonvolatile components. A short 20-pulse excitation produces an initial 70 pm resonance shift that relaxes toward baseline within approximately 60 s, with a volatile relaxation time constant of 27-29 s. In contrast, after 1000 pulses, an initial 0.27 nm resonance shift relaxes to a persistent 0.13 nm nonvolatile state that is retained for at least 24 h. Repeated 6 V electrical pulses produce a progressive resonance shift over 1000 cycles, demonstrating cumulative optical integration. A fixed-wavelength readout converts the accumulated resonance shift into a thresholded optical response, with the normalized transmission remaining above the selected threshold through 600 pulses and falling below it at the 800-pulse state. These dynamics realize the basis for a leaky integrate-and-fire photonic neuron, where the pulse-dependent ionic response provides integration, spontaneous relaxation supplies a passive leak, persistent states provide nonvolatile memory, and fixed-wavelength readout provides an optical threshold response.

authors.name: Ghada Dushaq, Srinivasa R. Tamalampudi, Mahmoud Rasras

papers.title: Speckle renewal, not bandwidth alone, mitigates kinetic Raman scattering at moderate bandwidth
papers.summary: Broadband lasers are expected to mitigate laser--plasma instabilities by shortening the coherence time. Using two-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations of kinetic Raman scattering, we compare two broadband beams with identical power spectra but different speckle dynamics. At 2% bandwidth, where Brillouin scattering is negligible, induced spatial incoherence (ISI) gives 34% less Raman backscatter than a broadband beam focused through a random phase plate (RPP+BB), an ordering that persists with immobile ions. The two fields differ in their finite-time speckle contrast.

authors.name: P. -E Masson-Laborde (CEA, LMCE), G Bouchard (CEA, LMCE), R Capdessus (CEA, LMCE), C Ruyer (CEA, LMCE), A Debayle (CEA, LMCE), A Fusaro (CEA, LMCE)

papers.title: Formation of Electron Velocity Distribution Functions at low-\{beta} Quasi-Perpendicular Shocks From Physical-Mass-Ratio PIC Simulations
papers.summary: At low-\{beta} quasi-perpendicular shocks, the origins of upstream field-aligned electron beams and downstream flat-top distributions remain unresolved. Using 2D fully kinetic particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations at the physical ion-to-electron mass ratio (mi/me = 1836), we found that the shock transition region is dominated by electromagnetic whistler-mode turbulence driven by the modified two-stream instability (MTSI) of reflected ions, not by the electrostatic instabilities as suggested by some previous studies using a reduced mass ratio. Beams in the upstream are produced mainly by shock-drift acceleration (SDA) at the ramp, whereas we attribute the downstream flat-top distributions to nonuniform acceleration by the parallel electric field. Electrons experience different field strengths, polarities, and interaction durations along their trajectories, leading to a spread of parallel velocity changes that broadens and flattens the distribution. These results highlight the importance of using the physical mass ratio in exploring the electron dynamics of low-\{beta} shocks.

authors.name: Zhoufan Mu, Yao Chen, Hao Ning, Shan Wang, Sibo Xu, Terry Zixu Liu, Ao Guo, Hui Zhang, Hui Zhu

papers.title: Dopamine: A Cartesian grid large-eddy-simulation framework for coastal ocean modelling of free-surface waves
papers.summary: We present a Cartesian staggered-grid large-eddy simulation framework for modelling coastal ocean waves using the Dopamine solver. The framework combines a geometric volume-of-fluid method for simulating free-surface wave evolution with one-way-coupled Lagrangian point-particle tracking for heavy and buoyant particles. A ghost-cell immersed-boundary method represents stationary solid boundaries, including the seabed and coastal obstacles, and their interaction with free-surface waves. The framework includes the Vreman and anisotropic minimum-dissipation (AMD) sub-grid-scale models for simulating near-wall turbulence. Comparisons with analytical solutions and established experimental and numerical benchmarks illustrate the framework's ability to reproduce wave dynamics and particle motion. The results provide promising insights into the framework's capabilities for coastal ocean modelling applications focused on investigating small-scale turbulent physics using a low-numerical-dissipation approach. The solver runs on multi-CPU architectures, with two-fluid strong- and weak-scaling efficiencies at 512 ranks relative to 64 ranks of up to 77% and 73%, respectively, and a single-GPGPU build has been verified against the CPU solver.

authors.name: Akshay Patil

papers.title: Gradient Optical Diffraction Tomography Using Deep Learning-Assisted Amplitude Estimation
papers.summary: Gradient Optical Diffraction Tomography (GODT) enables the non-invasive reconstruction of a spatial derivative of the 3D sample's refractive index distribution, providing enhanced sensitivity to subtle refractive index variations through gradient-based contrast. Implemented using lateral shearing interferometry (LSI), GODT benefits from a common-path architecture that provides environmental stability and high signal-to-noise ratio measurements. Unlike conventional optical diffraction tomography (ODT), which requires numerical integration of LSI-derived phase gradients to recover the object phase, GODT enables direct tomographic reconstruction from the LSI data. Notably, GODT requires derivatives of both the phase and amplitude of the object fields as input. While the phase derivative can be readily extracted from LSI data, the amplitude gradient cannot be directly retrieved. Thus, in the original GODT formulation, the amplitude gradient was assumed to be negligible, limiting the accuracy of the resulting 3D reconstruction. In this work, we introduce amplitude-informed GODT (AI-GODT), which employs physics-informed supervised deep learning to estimate the missing amplitude gradient based on accessible LSI data, specifically the fringe modulation. The proposed approach, applying a ResNet architecture and training on computer-generated data, is validated through numerical simulation and experimental measurements of both a well-characterized test object and primary neuronal cell culture, demonstrating the network's ability to generalize to diverse samples. We show that incorporation of the recovered amplitude gradient into the GODT reconstruction pipeline improves the 3D reconstruction quality, especially in its out-of-focus regions. The software and datasets are openly available to facilitate reproducibility and further development.

authors.name: Julianna Winnik (Institute of Micromechanics and Photonics, Warsaw University of Technology, Warsaw, Poland), Piotr Zda\'nkowski (Institute of Micromechanics and Photonics, Warsaw University of Technology, Warsaw, Poland), Konrad Kosuge (Institute of Micromechanics and Photonics, Warsaw University of Technology, Warsaw, Poland), Aleksandra Parys (Institute of Micromechanics and Photonics, Warsaw University of Technology, Warsaw, Poland), Marzena Stefaniuk (Laboratory of Neurobiology, BRAINCITY, Nencki Institute of Experimental Biology, Polish Academy of Sciences, Warsaw, Poland), Junwei Min (State Key Laboratory of Ultrafast Optical Science and Technology, Xi'an Institute of Optics and Precision Mechanics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Xi'an, China), Baoli Yao (State Key Laboratory of Ultrafast Optical Science and Technology, Xi'an Institute of Optics and Precision Mechanics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Xi'an, China, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China), Maciej Trusiak (Institute of Micromechanics and Photonics, Warsaw University of Technology, Warsaw, Poland)

papers.title: Pseudospin-mediated broadband hypersonic phonon transport beyond localized Berry curvature
papers.summary: Phononic nanostructures offer compact and highly confined control of elastic waves for signal transport, filtering, and quantum transduction. More recently, topological phononic structures have been explored as a route to robust waveguiding around defects and sharp bends, offering a promising basis for scalable and reliable phononic circuitry. However, how robust transport can persist as conventional localized Berry-curvature signatures diminish with increasing structural perturbation remains elusive. Here, we demonstrate bend-resilient hypersonic phonon transport beyond the conventional valley Hall framework. Using an engineered propeller phononic crystal operating at 1.9 GHz, we continuously increase the geometric perturbation to gradually weaken the valley topology while enhancing modal pseudospin character. Strikingly, as the Berry curvature progressively delocalizes from valleys, the complete elastic bandgap broadens to a normalized width of 34% and the interface modes become more strongly confined. Two-port electromechanical measurements on a thin-film lithium niobate-on-SOI platform experimentally confirm broadband interface-mode transport with no measurable bend-induced loss, despite the absence of well-localized valley-topology signatures. Our findings establish modal pseudospin engineering as a powerful design principle for robust acoustic guiding beyond conventional topological constraints, paving the way for broadband hypersonic phononic circuitry for classical and quantum information processing.

authors.name: Byunggi Kim, Michele Diego, Yohei Ogawara, Matteo Pirro, Hyuga Oka, Ryo Sasaki, Satoshi Iwamoto, Masahiro Nomura

papers.title: Mathematical modeling of regime-dependent thermal response in multilayer wall assemblies with equal total steady thermal resistance
papers.summary: Steady thermal resistance is a fundamental characteristic of building-envelope assemblies; however, equal steady resistance does not uniquely determine their transient thermal behavior. This study aims to numerically separate the effects of layer order, temperature-dependent thermophysical properties, and redistribution of thermal resistance between bulk and interfacial components in stationarily equivalent multilayer wall assemblies subjected to periodic and finite-pulse thermal loading. A one-dimensional transient heat-conduction model with Robin boundary conditions, finite interfacial thermal resistance, and source-supported temperature-dependent material properties was employed. All compared configurations were constrained to the same total steady thermal resistance at the reference temperature, $R_{\mathrm{tot}} = 3.65315$ m$^2$ K/W. The numerical implementation passed the adopted verification procedure with restrictions. The combined grid/time uncertainty was 0.325 %, below the prescribed 0.5 % acceptance criterion. For the tested pair differing only in layer order, the relative effect was -0.905 % for the periodic decrement factor and +0.566 % for the finite-pulse peak transmission ratio, with effect-to-uncertainty ratios of 79.2 and 88.9, respectively; the opposite signs therefore refer to two distinct regime-specific metrics. The temperature-dependent configuration produced a numerically resolved periodic effect of -2.005 %, whereas the corresponding pulse effect of -0.282 % remained below the adopted numerical-resolution threshold. For a compensated 5-10 % redistribution of bulk thermal resistance to interfacial contacts, the additional dynamic effect was likewise unresolved. The results demonstrate the value of controlled factor separation combined with explicit numerical-uncertainty assessment when evaluating transient thermal behavior.

authors.name: Dmytro Usenko, Valery Usenko, Iryna Usenko

papers.title: Minimum Effective-Susceptibility Bounds for Arbitrary Polarization Transformations in Metasurfaces
papers.summary: Metasurfaces are increasingly employed for sophisticated polarization transformations, including general unitary and nonunitary Jones operations. Despite substantial advances in analytical synthesis methods, inverse design of these transformations remains challenging. Here, we show that the particular mathematical structure of Jones polarization transformations makes optimal effective-susceptibility synthesis analytically tractable within the generalized sheet transition condition (GSTC) framework. For reciprocal, lossless dipolar metasurfaces, we establish exact feasibility and global minimum attainment, and derive sharp effective-susceptibility bounds for representative unitary and nonunitary transformations. We identify when magnetoelectric coupling lowers the minimum susceptibility, when it offers no resource advantage, and how the required material response depends on the prescribed polarization transformation. Applications to polarization rotations, tunable compensators, and polarization-state separation, including unambiguous discrimination, demonstrate sharp physical limits and material-resource trade-offs. These results provide geometry-independent theoretical benchmarks that can guide numerical inverse design and the selection of metasurface architectures.

authors.name: Ravi Hegde

papers.title: Bringing Singles to $GW$: A Coupled-Cluster Perspective on Orbital Relaxation
papers.summary: The one-shot $G_0W_0$ approximation suffers from a pronounced dependence on the underlying mean-field starting point. Here, we explore an alternative to conventional self-consistent $GW$ schemes by introducing single excitations within the recently established connection between $GW$ and extended coupled-cluster (ECC) theory. Starting from the equivalence between $G_0W_0$ and ionization-potential/electron-affinity equation-of-motion direct-ring extended coupled-cluster doubles (IP/EA-EOM-drECCD), we extend the formalism to include right-hand single-excitation and left-hand single-deexcitation cluster amplitudes coupled to the direct-ring doubles amplitudes. The resulting approximation, denoted singles-$G_0W_0$ (s$G_0W_0$), incorporates orbital-relaxation effects without explicitly introducing self-consistency in the Green's function. We assess the performance of s$G_0W_0$ for molecular valence and core ionization potentials using Hartree-Fock and Kohn-Sham starting points. For both types of ionizations, the inclusion of singles largely suppresses the starting-point dependence observed in conventional $G_0W_0$, yielding quasiparticle energies close to those obtained from the Hartree-Fock reference, irrespective of the initial mean-field description. Although this does not necessarily translate into improved absolute accuracy, it demonstrates that singles provide an effective route to reducing the starting-point dependence of $GW$-like approximations without resorting to self-consistency.

authors.name: Marios-Petros Kitsaras, Loris Burth, Pierre-Fran\c{c}ois Loos

papers.title: PineIR: 3D molecular structures from an infrared spectrum alone
papers.summary: Computing the infrared (IR) spectrum of a molecule from its structure is routine. The inverse problem is not. In practice, IR spectra are used to identify the functional groups present in a molecule, while the determination of its complete structure requires additional measurements. Machine-learning models that return 3D structures from IR spectra exist, but all of them need extra input, such as Raman, ultraviolet or nuclear magnetic resonance spectra, the molecular formula, or the number of atoms. In this work we present PineIR, a generative model that returns 3D molecular structures from the IR spectrum alone. PineIR builds the molecule atom by atom, and each atom is associated with its contribution to the IR spectrum. This contribution is subtracted from the input spectrum before the next atom is generated. To train it, we computed with a machine-learned interatomic potential the IR spectra of 4.6 million structures of 3.1 million molecules, including conformer ensembles. On computed spectra of held-out molecules, the best-ranked of fifty candidates has the correct connectivity in 43% of the cases, and the generated geometries reproduce the conformer and the diastereomer that produced the input spectrum. After fine-tuning on 161k spectra calculated with the hybrid functional B3LYP, the model can also be applied to spectra at this level of theory.

authors.name: Giulio Benedini, Pierre-Paul De Breuck, Miguel A. L. Marques, Silvana Botti

papers.title: Angular dependence of the Wigner time delay upon tunnel ionization of CO
papers.summary: We report on Wigner time delays in the strong-field ionization of carbon monoxide. Using co-rotating two-color laser fields (395 and 790 nm), we retrieve time delays that depend on the electron emission direction in the molecular frame, with variations of up to $\pm70$ as. The measured angular dependence agrees with predictions from a simple model based on molecular Ammosov-Delone-Krainov (MO-ADK) theory. Our results demonstrate that the directional dependence of electron emission times in asymmetric molecular potentials can be experimentally accessed in the strong-field regime.

authors.name: N. Anders, A. Geyer, M. Hofmann, D. Trabert, J. Stindl, N. L. Wong, J. Kruse, S. Jacob, M. S. Sch\"offler, L. Ph. H. Schmidt, T. Jahnke, M. Kunitski, S. Eckart

papers.title: Fourier-Transform Photothermal Spectroscopy with Transient-Lens Detection
papers.summary: We demonstrate Fourier-transform photothermal spectroscopy using broadband supercontinuum excitation and transient-lens detection. The output of a Ti:sapphire oscillator is broadened in a photonic crystal fiber to generate the supercontinuum pump, which is converted into a phase-stable pulse pair with a controllable femtosecond delay using a birefringent interferometer. The absorption-induced heating from the pump generates a transient thermal lens in the sample, which is detected as a function of delay by an off-resonant 800 nm photothermal probe beam. Fourier transform of the interferometric photothermal response yields a frequency-domain signal corresponding to the sample absorptance spectrum weighted by the pump spectrum. After division by the measured pump spectrum, the reconstructed photothermal spectrum is compared with a direct frequency-domain linear absorption measurement to evaluate the accuracy of the reconstruction. This method combines Fourier-transform broadband excitation with thermal-lens readout, allowing broadband linear absorption spectra to be obtained from pump-induced refractive-index changes rather than from transmitted excitation intensity. We demonstrate the method on phloxine B.

authors.name: Asha S. Thomas, Toluwatomi Haastrup, Luzhou Yu, Muyi Zhang, Jennifer P. Ogilvie

papers.title: Numerical model for ice formation in soil samples
papers.summary: Ice formation, or in general liquid crystallization, in porous media is important in various engineering contexts ranging from frost heave in soils to structural damage due to salt crystallization. Developing mesoscopic models for this problem is challenging due to the multitude of phenomena involved - fluid flow, phase transitions and complex porous geometries. In this work, we present an efficient numerical implementation addressing this class of problems. We use a phase field model with a non-conserved order parameter for liquid crystallization and solve it in a Lattice-Boltzmann framework. Our modifications to the phase field model enable the direct capture of important thermodynamic phenomena such as the Gibbs-Thomson effect and Soil Freezing Characteristic Curve (SFCC). We demonstrate our model's capabilities in sphere packings as well as in realistic soil geometries. Our model is able to resolve the pore-scale freezing and capture the macroscopic freezing behavior such as the hysteresis observed during freezing and thawing.

authors.name: Varghese Babu, Dilip Gersappe

papers.title: Unveiling gauge-invariant on-chip phases from light intensity
papers.summary: Physics-informed digital twins fitted to output powers increasingly program photonic processors, but these powers do not fix the implemented phase, which determines how light from different inputs interferes. Here we show that a twin trained on intensities alone predicts the gauge-invariant phase of programmed transformations, and that this prediction can be used to program the phase. On a $12\times12$ mesh, with phases measured by interference protocols formed by the mesh itself, intensity-only and phase-aware programs from random starts reach the same intensity fidelity but phase fidelities of 0.690 and 0.996, both as predicted by the twin. The prediction holds for blocks up to $10\times10$. With coherent inputs, the programmed phase determines the outputs: phase-aware programming reduces the direction-of-arrival error of an on-chip Butler matrix from 29 degrees to 2.0 degrees. Power measurements alone thus yield a phase-calibrated model of the mesh, without phase data in training or optics beyond the chip.

authors.name: Huiwen Li, Andrea Cataldo, Rohan Yadgirkar, Jun Gao, Ali W. Elshaari

papers.title: Producing and Measuring Circularly Polarized X-rays: A Jones and Mueller-Stokes Treatment of Crystal Phase Plates
papers.summary: Converting a linearly polarized X-ray beam into a circularly polarized one, and then verifying the polarization state actually delivered, are standard operations at synchrotron radiation facilities. The key optical element is a quarter-wave plate (QWP), a birefringent crystal that introduces a 90-degree (quarter-wavelength) phase retardation between the two orthogonal components of the electric field. This paper presents a self-contained theoretical treatment of X-ray polarization optics. We first establish the Jones and Mueller-Stokes formalisms and their connection via the Pauli matrices, fixing the sign and handedness conventions explicitly and reconciling them with those used elsewhere in the literature. From there we derive the Jones and Mueller matrices of a general retarder at an arbitrary orientation angle chi (including the QWP that converts horizontal linear polarization into circular polarization of either handedness) and of linear polarizers, and describe the experimental Stokes polarimetry protocol used at synchrotron beamlines. These results are then combined to treat the general crystal phase plate, characterized by two complex reflection (or transmission) amplitudes r_s and r_p, obtaining the degree of circular polarization delivered for an arbitrary incident beam as a function of chi and the phase retardation delta. Finally, we turn to the practical implementation of these elements with perfect-crystal diffraction: the residual polarization impurity of a Brewster-angle polarizer and the role of ray tracing in evaluating it, and the choice of diffraction geometry (Bragg or Laue, diffracted or transmitted beam) for obtaining a significant, controllable phase shift. The formalism presented here is the mathematical background of the treatment of polarization in the ray-tracing code SHADOW4.

authors.name: Manuel Sanchez del Rio, Carsten Detlefs

papers.title: Funding Landscape of Early-Career Scientists: A Perspective from the AGU SPA Early Career Leadership Advisory Committee
papers.summary: Like researchers across many scientific fields, early-career researchers in heliophysics face a critical transition from supervised research to independent scientific inquiry. However, the funding landscape that should support this transition is fragmented and unpredictable. Here we examine the current funding opportunities available to early-career researchers in heliophysics alongside the historical experiences of established scientists who navigated similar transitions. We catalog the major U.S. federal programs targeting early-career space physicists, documenting their eligibility constraints, selection rates, and accessibility. Access varies with career stage, appointment type, citizenship requirements, and solicitation schedules, and selection rates can swing sharply: the NASA Heliophysics Early Career Investigator Program (ECIP) selected 28% of proposals in 2022 but only 6% in 2024. To provide historical context, we collected survey responses from 30 researchers whose PhDs span 1972-2016 and conducted eight interviews with mid- and senior-career researchers. Most respondents viewed the present funding environment as more difficult than their own early careers, identifying predictability of opportunity, not ease, as what enabled earlier generations to build independence. Salary support alone does not guarantee opportunities to develop scientific leadership; accessible PI awards and real responsibility within collaborative projects can both contribute to that development. We recommend predictable, adequately sized grant programs for early-career principal investigators, transparent reporting of selection statistics across all early-career programs, continued use of dual-anonymous peer review, and named leadership roles for early-career researchers within large projects.

authors.name: Savvas Raptis, Claire Gasque, Samuel Hart, Yi Qi, Chris R. Gilly, B. L. Alterman, Ryan M. McGranaghan, Juan Camilo Buitrago-Casas, Komal Kumari, Garima Malhotra, Parisa Mostafavi, Eduardo Perez Macho, Onyinye Nwankwo-Omoloja

papers.title: Optimization of a Locally Shielded 16-Channel Transmit Array for Human Brain MRI at 10.5 T via Electromagnetic/Circuit Co-Simulation and Parallel Transmission Strategies
papers.summary: Modern neuroimaging and neuroscience increasingly demand high spatial and temporal resolution, driving the use of ultrahigh-field (7 T and above) MRI for improved signal-to-noise ratio. Realizing this advantage depends critically on advanced radiofrequency (RF) and gradient technologies, particularly multi-channel transmit arrays and high-performance head-gradient systems. In integrated systems, a local RF shield must provide sufficient field confinement while preserving transmit performance and minimizing sensitivity to nearby conductive structures. In this work, we sought to optimize a locally shielded 16-channel transmit RF array for human neuroimaging at 10.5 T using electromagnetic/circuit co-simulation combined with parallel-transmission strategies. Candidate transmit-array and RF-shield configurations were evaluated before and after gradient-shield integration to identify a configuration with suitable RF transmit and shielding performance for the integrated system. The results show that no single standalone metric, including static RF shimming performance, dynamic parallel transmission (pTx) performance, or external-field leakage, reliably predicts robustness after gradient-shield integration. Progressive screening identified the aligned loop-folded dipole (LFD) array combined with a compact cylindrical shield featuring a conical top and three windows (160-mm radius and 70-mm window length) as the final configuration. Without RF-circuit retuning, the selected design maintained external-field leakage below 1% and after gradient shield integration achieved whole-brain excitation coefficient of variation (CoV) of approximately 27% with static RF shimming and 9% with dynamic pTx. Experimental validation of the unshielded LFD array showed good agreement between simulated and measured B1+ efficiency distributions, with a normalized root-mean-square error (NRMSE) of approximately 8%.

authors.name: Mengxuan Zheng, Xin Shao, Matt Waks, Mazin M. Mustafa, Kamil Ugurbil, Xiaoping Wu, Xiaotong Zhang, Alireza Sadeghi-Tarakameh

papers.title: Full-waveform inversion with adaptive anisotropic Gaussian primitives
papers.summary: Reparameterizing the velocity model has emerged as an effective way to regularize full-waveform inversion (FWI) and reduce its sensitivity to the starting model. Existing parameterizations, however, either fix the position and shape of every basis function in advance, as in grids and splines, or control the spatial structure of their updates only indirectly through the shared weights of a neural network. We propose Gauss-FWI, which represents the velocity perturbation as a sum of anisotropic Gaussian primitives with learnable amplitudes, centres, scales, and orientations. The basis itself thus adapts to the subsurface. Primitives move onto interfaces, stretch along layers, and rotate with the dip, so model updates follow the geological structure without a hand-designed regularizer. A gradient-energy criterion adds finer zero-amplitude primitives where the data call for more detail, increasing resolution progressively without perturbing the current model. All parameters receive analytic gradients through the adjoint-state method on a fixed simulation grid, so the representation fits into existing FWI workflows and combines directly with frequency continuation. Each primitive keeps an explicit position, extent, and orientation, and the representation Jacobian links the waveform gradient to the resulting model update, which makes the behaviour of the inversion interpretable. In two-dimensional acoustic examples, Gauss-FWI uses about fifty times fewer parameters than implicit FWI and recovers the Marmousi, Overthrust, and BP salt models more accurately than grid, multiscale, B-spline, and implicit parameterizations. It remains accurate under missing low frequencies, noise, and discretization mismatch, and it recovers the main structure from starting models where the other methods fail, such as a linear model without the BP salt body.

authors.name: Pu Yang, Yuxin Liu, Zhengyang Fang, Bin Zhang, Deshan Feng

papers.title: Solitons as conversion events in quadratic crystals
papers.summary: In a $\chi^{(2)}$ crystal with temporal walk-off and negligible dispersion, signal, idler and pump pulses obey the integrable three-wave interaction. For a pump of intermediate group velocity we describe each soliton as a conversion event: the fusion of a signal--idler pair into a pump pulse, or the decay of a pump pulse, at a definite depth in the crystal. The asymptotic $\mathrm{sech}$ pulses, usually treated with three separate $2\times2$ scattering problems, are the legs of the event, a single pole of the $3\times3$ problem. For one event we give the conversion curve in closed form and the minimum crystal length; for several events, the rule by which they displace each other. A pump pulse is unstable, and its growing mode is the tail of a decay event: a seed carrying a fraction $\varepsilon$ of the photons along this mode makes the pulse decay after $\Gamma^{-1}\ln(c_+/\varepsilon)$, with $\Gamma$ the conversion rate and $c_+$ of order one. Unmatched signal and idler pulses form the resonance of Kaup, Reiman and Bers; we show that it is a fusion followed by a decay, each within a conversion length, and give its pump photon number in closed form. Since the delay between the input pulses sets the depth of the vertex, these quantities can be read on the output face of a single crystal; we give the scales for periodically poled KTiOPO$_4$.

authors.name: Francesco Beccarini, Claudio Conti

papers.title: Uphill Diffusion in Yukawa Plasmas
papers.summary: In a fluid mixture of many species an individual species can diffuse toward higher concentration without any external driving force because its flux is coupled to the gradients of other components. Such `uphill diffusion' is well known in the chemical and metallurgy literature but to our knowledge has not been studied for strongly coupled plasmas in neutron star and white dwarf interiors. We have previously developed a semi-analytic diffusion model that accurately predicts diffusion coefficients of individual species in a mixture in equilibrium. Uphill diffusion allows us to test this model out of equilibrium, and also test a generalized Darken relation for predicting diffusivities. We derive an analytic theory and compare to three-component molecular dynamics simulations and find very good agreement. This provides a novel out-of-equilibrium test of the generalization of our diffusion model to arbitrary multi-component mixtures.

authors.name: Matt E. Caplan, Evan B. Bauer, Mohammed Bettioua

papers.title: StePPO: Adaptive Step-Size Control for Initial-Value Problems Using Proximal Policy Optimisation
papers.summary: ODE solvers are used to model, simulate, and analyse continuous-time systems found in many signal processing applications. Time integration of these initial-value problems is traditionally performed using adaptive embedded Runge--Kutta methods. For proper time-step selection, adaptive solvers accept or reject each candidate step according to a local error estimate. Their efficiency is therefore controlled by the rule that selects the next step size. Classical proportional--integral--derivative (PID) controllers are computationally inexpensive per decision and reliable, but their reactive design can lead to costly numerical solves near stiff transitions. We formulate step-size selection for parametrised IVPs as a Markov decision process and train a continuous-action policy using proximal policy optimisation. The policy processes its observation signals using a deep network while maintaining the embedded solver logic. We evaluate on a decay function, the Van der Pol system, and the Brusselator system at matched tolerances, and compare against a standard PID controller and a multi-scale DeepONet network. We find that the proposed learned policy remains within prescribed error tolerances while reducing the required number of solve steps by up to 60%, achieving a wall-clock time reduction of 58%, for both in- and out-of-distribution settings.

authors.name: Milan Koumans, Nicola Pezzotti, Tristan S. W. Stevens

papers.title: A Monolithic Fully Eulerian Lattice Boltzmann Framework for Fluid--Structure Interaction with Neo-Hookean Elastic Solids
papers.summary: We present a fully Eulerian, monolithic lattice Boltzmann method for fluid--structure interaction with incompressible neo-Hookean solids at unequal densities, and use it to compute the Turek--Hron FSI2 and FSI3 benchmarks on a single Cartesian grid. A pressure-based kinetic scheme advances the mixture momentum, a polynomial MTHINC reconstruction transports the solid volume fraction with closed-form fluxes, and the left Cauchy--Green tensor gives the elastic stress; all updates are explicit and local. Because the density is transported independently of the populations, two corrections are introduced. A lattice-link correction makes uniform translation an exact discrete solution for any density ratio, which is verified to round-off up to $\rho_s/\rho_f=1000$. A pressure-mode correction, derived from an asymptotic analysis of the scheme, removes the frame-dependent defect that otherwise causes a secular drift of the solid mass. The verification separates the two sources of error: the scheme is second-order accurate towards the diffuse-interface solution at fixed interface thickness, and first-order towards the sharp-interface solution when the thickness scales with the grid, as predicted by an estimate of the interfacial truncation error. The method reproduces a deformable disk in Taylor--Green and lid-driven-cavity flows, and the FSI3 and FSI2 benchmarks at density ratios of one and ten.

authors.name: Tristan Millet, Erwan Liberge

papers.title: Site-Resolved Optical Spectroscopy of Thulium in Solid Argon
papers.summary: We utilize the high resolution of the ground state transition ${}^2\mathrm{F}_{7/2} \leftrightarrow {}^2\mathrm{F}_{5/2}$ in thulium atoms isolated in solid argon to perform excitation-emission spectroscopy. Decomposition of the excitation-emission spectrum reveals 6 absorption-emission profiles, which are attributed to multiple trapping sites in the host matrix. Comparison with vacuum transition energies shows large matrix-induced shifts for $\mathrm{s}\rightarrow\mathrm{p}$ transitions, whereas $\mathrm{f} \rightarrow \mathrm{d}$ transitions remain close to their free-atom energies. A single site exhibiting strong emission at 560nm is investigated and a three-photon excitation pathway is determined as a possible origin of the high energy 560nm light. Additionally, for long-lived levels belonging to the $\mathrm{f}^{12}\mathrm{d}$ configuration, narrow, crystal-field split absorption lines are identified. Matrix effects are important for establishing the mechanism behind the observed spectra and long $\mathrm{f}^{12}\mathrm{d}$ lifetimes.

authors.name: Jason Marfey, Heming Gao, Colin V. Parker

papers.title: Arbitrarily Weak Losses Destroy Fractal Bandstructure in Temporal Fibonacci Quasicrystals
papers.summary: Lossless photonic crystals with weak refractive index contrasts block limited frequencies. However, the same materials arranged in a non-periodic Fibonacci quasicrystal block all but infinitely rare fractally-distributed frequencies. Similar analysis shows that weak quasiperiodic refractive index variation in time should achieve infinitely broadband gain. We demonstrate that any small experimental losses immediately destroy this effect. Our methods also provide smoothness and approximation theorems for the localisation lengths central to topology in spatial problems.

authors.name: Calvin M. Hooper

papers.title: CLM-JAX v3.2.46: a differentiable, GPU-accelerated land surface model numerically indistinguishable from the Community Land Model 5.0
papers.summary: The original Fortran implementation of the Community Land Model version 5.0 (CLM5.0) primarily targets CPUs and does not support GPU computation or automatic differentiation. We present CLM-JAX, a land surface model implemented in Python, based on the CLM5.0 BGC-Crop configuration in the Community Earth System Model version 2.1.3 (CESM2.1.3). CLM-JAX retains the original subgrid hierarchy, parameterizations and coupling among energy, water, carbon, nitrogen and crop processes, runs on CPUs and GPUs, and supports gradient backpropagation through multi-step time integration. Using floating-point perturbations of order $10^{-14}$ in the initial state, we construct a stringent ensemble baseline of CLM's own differences and evaluate the numerical consistency of CLM-JAX for 32 variables over five years of continuous global simulation during 2019-2023. CLM-JAX errors relative to CLM generally lie below this ensemble baseline. On a single NVIDIA A800 GPU, CLM-JAX requires 0.7692 s per model hour, yielding sustained integration speedups of 4.04 and 2.57 over CLM compiled with gfortran and ifort, respectively, on 64 CPU cores. In the gradient test, the objective function is the first-layer soil temperature at step 100 (50 h), and its gradient with respect to the initial soil temperature field of all model layers is obtained by backpropagation through the 100 time steps. With converged central finite differences as references, 95.79% of the 84,254 nonzero references have relative errors no greater than 1% and 98.22% have matching signs, with median and 90th-percentile relative errors of $5.862\times10^{-7}$% and $3.578\times10^{-4}$%, respectively. The differentiability of CLM-JAX provides a basis for gradient-based applications, such as end-to-end parameter optimization and four-dimensional variational data assimilation.

authors.name: Shijin Yuan, Zhen Wei, Tianyu Shen, Bin Mu, Bo Qin, Guokun Dai

papers.title: Theory of Observability of Voigt-Wave Propagation in a Homogeneous Dielectric Material
papers.summary: A Voigt wave can propagate in a dissipative anisotropic dielectric material when a 4$\times$4 propagation matrix is defective, as happens for a uniform plane wave along a singular axis, and the field depends on the propagation distance linearly as well as exponentially. Whether it is observable outside a slab of that material generally depends on whether the defectiveness is inherited by the 2$\times$2 reflection and transmission matrices, which are extracted from the 2$\times$2 blocks of a 4$\times$4 transfer matrix that relates the fields at the two faces of the slab. Explicit tests exist for each type of defectiveness, and a counting argument shows that excitation and observability co-occur at oblique incidence only for isolated combinations of constitutive parameters and slab thickness. Normal incidence is exceptional: Voigt-wave excitation then generally implies a defective transmission matrix for almost all thicknesses, which explains Voigt's 1902 experiment on andalusite. Numerical searches for andalusite, $\beta$-gallium oxide, terbium orthoaluminate in a magnetostatic field, and hexagonal boron nitride show that a Voigt wave may be excited without being observable and that a defective reflection or transmission matrix need not signal the excitation of a Voigt wave.

authors.name: Akhlesh Lakhtakia, Tom G. Mackay

papers.title: Pressure demand and solute replacement in a collagen-plugged bioreactor
papers.summary: In a perfusion bioreactor, fresh culture medium enters through a small opening, flows through a collagen plug, and leaves through a second opening. How much pressure is needed to sustain that flow? When fresh medium reaches the outlet, has it also replaced the old medium inside the pores? To answer these questions, we simulated flow and medium replacement in pores traced from a collagen image. The flow simulations and curved-channel theory show how narrow, winding passages concentrate resistance. We used that resistance to estimate the plug permeability and found that the modeled plug accounts for most of the pressure drop across the chamber. Feeding through small openings adds to that demand because the flow must spread through the plug and converge again at the outlet. At the same flow rate, this requires about seven times the pressure needed with uniform feeding across the plug faces. Pore shape also affects how closely the outlet signal tracks replacement in the interior. In most runs, the interior reaches 99% replacement before the outlet does. A slowly exchanging side pocket can reverse that order by retaining old medium while fresh medium passes through the main channel. In the strongest case, the interior takes nearly three times as long as the outlet to reach the same replacement threshold.

authors.name: Mohammad Mehedi Hasan Akash, Mohammad Yeasin, Karl Van Horsen, Mithul Sathish, Susan Immanuel, Sanku Mallik, Saikat Basu

papers.title: Tunable Terahertz Bandpass Filter based on the Photonic Emulation of a 2DEG Interferometer through the Geometric Phase of Light
papers.summary: Terahertz frequencies are expected to become a key player in next-generation wireless communications. For this transition to occur seamlessly, tunable bandpass filters for channel selection are essential. However, conventional Fabry-P\'erot cavity-based bandpass filters face inherent limitations. Specifically, their tunability is restricted by physical constraints, such as the maximum achievable mirror separation. In this work, drawing inspiration from electronic interferometers, we demonstrate a continuously tunable bandpass filter operating near 0.3 THz by exploiting the geometric phase of light, the Pancharatnam-Berry phase. Our device incorporates intracavity waveplates for polarization control and is described by a mathematical expression analogous to that of the electronic interferometer governed by the Aharonov-Bohm phase, thereby realizing a photonic analogue. Using custom-designed subwavelength waveplates and cavity mirrors, we achieve a finesse of $\mathcal{F}\approx17$, a quality factor of $Q\approx1.5\times10^{3}$, and a resonance linewidth of $\Delta f_{\mathrm{FWHM}}\approx 200$ MHz. Beyond terahertz communication technology, this system is expected to find applications in fields requiring high frequency resolution, such as spectroscopy.

authors.name: Victor I. Iwanaga, Hiroaki Shirasaka, Shin'ichiro Hayashi, Katsuhiko Miyamoto, Yoshiharu Urata, Kouji Nawata, Jun-ichi Shikata, Norihiko Sekine, Seigo Ohno

papers.title: Fewer Fractions, Equieffective Plans: An optimization framework based on equieffective dose
papers.summary: Background: Non-standard fractionation requires caution before clinical use, and planners often need to manually modify the prescription and dose constraints for non-linear biological effects. Purpose: To develop an extension within a treatment planning system that enables the generation of hypofractionated plans based on equieffective dose, $EQD_{n_{ref}}$, for an alternative fractionation deliverable in $n$ fractions, such that it is equieffective with the reference fractionation for a specified biological endpoint. Methods: A research build of RayStation v2025 was extended to optimize $EQD_{n_{ref}}$ plans. This study used anonymized data from three head and neck patients. $\text{CTV}_p$ and $\text{CTV}_n$ were prescribed 70 Gy and 54 Gy in 35 fractions. Targets, spinal cord, and brainstem were robustly optimized for $\pm3.5$% density and $\pm3.0$ mm setup uncertainties. For each patient, hypofractionated plans were created with 34, 32, 30, and 25 fractions. Sensitivity analysis evaluated the impact of $\alpha/\beta$ uncertainty. Results: All equieffective hypofractionated plans maintained target coverage and met mandatory clinical goals for organs-at-risk (OARs). Compared to standard fractionation, DVH parameters indicated an average $\Delta EQD_{n_{ref}}$ <0.2 Gy for $\text{CTV}_p$ and no difference for $\text{CTV}_n$. For parallel OARs, the median mean-dose difference between hypofractionation (to 30 fractions) and standard fractionation was generally <1% of the prescribed dose. $\alpha/\beta$ uncertainty produced the greatest variation in the 25-fraction regimen, with absolute $\Delta EQD_{n_{ref}}$ up to 0.88 Gy for targets and up to 0.63 Gy for the spinal cord and brainstem. Conclusions: An $EQD_{n_{ref}}$-based framework can generate equieffective hypofractionated plans, making it feasible to reduce fractions without substantially deviating from existing clinical protocols.

authors.name: Suryakant Kaushik, Jakob \"Od\'en, Albin Fredriksson, Iuliana Toma-Dasu

papers.title: Stochastic Failure Dynamics in a Model Peptidoglycan Mesh under Hydrolysis and Mechanical Loading
papers.summary: We develop a minimal stochastic-mechanical model for failure dynamics of the Gram-negative peptidoglycan (PG) cell wall under blocked growth and continued hydrolysis. The cell wall is modelled as a collection of load-bearing cross-sections, with random number of cross-links in each such cross-section, around a fixed degree of cross-linking. To understand failure dynamics of the cell wall under antibacterial agents which prevent insertion of fresh PG material, peptide bonds are progressively excised by hydrolases, while insertion/formation of new bonds is blocked. We compare and contrast rupture dynamics in no-load and load-activated regimes, using extreme value theory and stochastic simulations, deriving limiting laws for system failure in both the long-cell and large crosslinking limits. For a cross-section with many bonds, the mean failure time grows only log- arithmically with bond number, giving diminishing returns from additional cross-linking. In the no-load case, the centered failure time converges to a Gumbel law, though crucially, load changes the centered distribution and accelerates the final stages of collapse. In long cells, failure follows a weakest-link Weibull-type scaling controlled by the least cross-linked regions, with mechanical load reducing the failure-time scale without changing the weakest-link exponent. The fraction of bonds removed before failure tends to zero, showing that collapse can remain highly localized even while the global cross-linking degree stays high. Slowing down growth and other cellular functions is a typical antibiotic escape mechanism for bacteria and in this context, we show that, hydrolase down-regulation uniformly rescales the failure-time distribution and delays collapse, but does not remove the load-induced preference for rupture in weakened regions.

authors.name: Issan Patri, Garima Rani

papers.title: Source Detection in Complex Networks: Observability, Identifiability, and Inference Frameworks
papers.summary: Tracing diffusion to its origin is a central inverse problem in complex networks, with applications ranging from epidemic investigation and information spreading to cyber incidents and disruptions in interconnected systems. Although source-detection methods have advanced along diverse methodological lines, their capabilities cannot be assessed independently of the evidence on which they operate. Network structure and diffusion dynamics determine which propagation histories are possible, while the observation mechanism determines which traces of those histories are retained. This review develops an information-centric and identifiability-aware perspective that connects these elements to source inference. We organize existing research around three overlapping observation settings: complete state snapshots, incomplete or noisy observations, and sensor-based observation and design. Within this organization, we examine structural, probabilistic, message-passing, simulation-based, and learning-based methods, comparing their required inputs, underlying assumptions, inference mechanisms, and computational demands. System-theoretic observability, statistical identifiability, and information-theoretic constraints provide complementary ways to examine what the available observations can reveal, while separating limitations of the evidence from those of estimation. Drawing on applications across epidemiological, information, biological, neural, and socioeconomic systems, we identify challenges in uncertainty assessment, model robustness, transfer across networks, and the acquisition of informative observations. This synthesis clarifies the conditions under which diffusion sources can be identified and how inference methods should be selected according to the available observations.

authors.name: Xiu-Xiu Zhan, Qiao Ke, Chengjun Zhang, Miao He, Chenwei Xie, Seba Contreras, Zhongliang Zhao, Yixiu Kong, Cong Li, Chuang Liu

papers.title: Electrostatic effects on settling cloud droplets: from pair collisions to size distribution evolution
papers.summary: We investigate how droplet charge and a uniform vertical electric field influence collisions between cloud droplets settling in still air and how these collisions shape the droplet size distribution. We compute collision efficiencies by analyzing the relative trajectories of pairs of spherical, conducting droplets, accounting for droplet inertia, exact hydrodynamic, electrostatic, and van der Waals forces. The hydrodynamic interactions are based on exact two-body solutions for Stokes flow with interfacial mobility and internal circulation. In the absence of an applied electric field, collisions between like-charged droplets are suppressed, whereas collisions between oppositely-charged droplets are enhanced. A vertical electric field promotes collisions between uncharged droplets through induced polarization and, when sufficiently strong, can overcome the repulsion between like-charged droplets. When the larger droplet has a radius of $10$ or $20\mu$m raising the electric field strength from $5\times10^{4}$ to $3\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$ can enhance the collision efficiency of uncharged droplet pairs by an order of magnitude. Depending on droplet size and field strength, for oppositely charged pairs, an applied electric field can either enhance or suppress collisions relative to the zero-field case. Using collision kernels computed from droplet pair trajectories, we solve the stochastic collection equation with a flux method on a two-dimensional grid that resolves droplet mass and charge. For an initial mean droplet radius of $10\mu$m , by $40$ min in every electrified case the large-droplet mode of the mass spectrum reaches a larger radius than in the hydrodynamic reference case. This suggests that electrostatic interactions can hasten warm rain initiation by accelerating droplet growth through collision and coalescence.

authors.name: Pijush Patra, John S. Wettlaufer

papers.title: Automatic dual basis sets for self-consistent field calculations
papers.summary: Density functional theory (DFT) has long been the workhorse of electronic structure theory, and it is experiencing a new boom thanks to big data applications and machine learning. A DFT calculation requires the iterative solution of the self-consistent field (SCF) problem, whose cost is the product of (i) the number of SCF steps and (ii) the cost of a single step. The number of SCF steps depends strongly on the initial guess, regardless of the SCF algorithm, and quantitative DFT accuracy is known to require at least a polarized triple-$\zeta$ basis set. However, a qualitatively correct solution may often be found already in a smaller \emph{dual basis} (DB), which can then bootstrap a calculation in the full basis set. Traditionally, the DB is chosen by hand for each application to enable robust convergence to the ground state. In this work, we pursue automatic generation of DBs for SCF calculations. Our generator constructs a pruned orbital basis from the target orbital basis for a predefined precision threshold and a given Fock matrix. As expected, the larger the basis set is, the smaller the fraction of kept basis functions. The DBs produced by our algorithm exhibit similar performance for a wide range of systems from the first 4 periods of the periodic table. Ultimately, we find that presently available initial guesses for the Fock matrix are not accurate enough to unlock the use of adaptive basis sets, and believe that the same limitation may hold for similar attempts for basis compactification.

authors.name: Joonatan Huhtasalo, Susi Lehtola

papers.title: Diagnosing internal leakage currents through magnetometry of lithium-ion cells
papers.summary: Internal leakage currents are difficult to detect and to localize through measurements at the terminals of lithium-ion cells. We measured the magnetic fields of pouch cells non-invasively with a magnetometer while a battery cycler set the current and recorded the voltage. A three-axis magnetoresistive sensor remains fixed inside a three-layer magnetic shield, and two linear stages move the cell in two dimensions relative to the sensor to acquire a map of the magnetic field above the cell. The field of an intact cell was linear in current from 10 to 420 mA, and its maps were symmetric between charge and discharge. To create internal leakage currents, two 600 mAh cells were damaged by mechanical indentation. Both cells developed a magnetic field at zero applied current that decayed over hours, while the cell voltage showed a loss of charge by self-discharge. This field breaks the symmetry between the charge and discharge maps, which allows leakage to be detected while the cell is being cycled. At rest, the setup detects leakage currents down to about 1--3 mA. The results highlight opportunities for battery diagnostics and safety, and may help in designing techniques for characterizing soft shorts.

authors.name: Shaurya Shukla, Chengtong Zhang, Yinan Hu, Stefan Benders, Mykhailo Flaks, Dmitry Budker, Alexej Jerschow

papers.title: A 2D fluid model in BOUT++/Hermes-3 for simulating detached divertor plasmas in tokamaks
papers.summary: Detached divertor operation is essential for controlling target heat fluxes in future high-power tokamaks. We present a two-dimensional fluid model implemented in BOUT++/Hermes-3 for simulating detached divertor plasmas with plasma-neutral interactions and fixed-fraction impurity radiation. We report improvements to the PETSc SNES-based steady-state solver used for two-dimensional axisymmetric transport simulations with fluid neutrals and assess the performance of several sparse-solver preconditioning strategies. For the cases considered here, STRUMPACK used as an ILU preconditioner with low-rank compression provides the most favorable performance, reducing the linear-to-nonlinear iteration ratio and achieving approximately a fivefold speedup relative to \HYPRE{}-based configurations. The optimized solver is then applied to DIII-D shot $\#174287$ at 4000~ms to characterize detached divertor conditions. Cross-field transport coefficients are adjusted to reproduce upstream experimental profiles, and detachment is modeled using nitrogen fixed-fraction radiation. Steady-state particle and energy balances are evaluated by decomposing the density and pressure equations into their transport and source terms. In the outer divertor, electron energy losses are dominated by ionization and impurity radiation, while ion energy losses occur mainly through collisional transfer to electrons. An upstream separatrix density scan shows decreasing target electron temperature and a rollover of the integrated target ion saturation current at higher $n_{e,\mathrm{sep}}$ consistent with expected detachment trends. These developments establish a foundation for future multispecies simulations. Hermes-3 is publicly available on GitHub under the GPL-3 open-source license.

authors.name: Malamas Tsagkaridis, Ben Dudson, Mike Kryjak, Nami Li, Xueqiao Xu

papers.title: Observation of a F\"orster Resonance in a Heated Rydberg Atom Ensemble
papers.summary: Rydberg atoms in thermal vapour are of increasing relevance for a range of emerging technologies including compact electric field sensors, where state energies are detected via electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT). However, at increased atomic number densities, the Rydberg EIT response becomes non-linear, resulting in distortion of the spectral lineshape. It is thought that this non-linearity mainly arises due to ionisation, although accurate quantitative modelling of the spectrum and assessment of other physical processes remains challenging. In this work, we address these issues in a combined theoretical and experimental study, constructing a model that accurately reproduces observed EIT spectral profiles. We show from analysis of lineshape shifts that while ionisation accounts for most of the non-linearity, it is also possible to observe Rydberg interaction effects for strongly-coupled states near a F\"orster resonance.

authors.name: Richard G. Wolfendale, Philipp L. K\"ohler, Karen Wadenpfuhl, Robert L. Mellor, Jake Hulse, Kevin J. Weatherill, Aaron Reinhard, C. Stuart Adams

papers.title: A general-purpose electron density model for molecular chemistry
papers.summary: Universal machine-learning potentials predict molecular structure and stability at the accuracy of quantum mechanics, for a fraction of the cost. Properties derived instead from knowledge of the electronic structure give profound insights into chemical reactivity, but are not accessible with the same ease or transferability. We train PET-rho-OMol25, a model of the ground-state electron density and spin polarization of molecular systems on four million OMol25 structures in multiple charge and spin states. The model makes predictions for entire proteins in a few seconds on a single GPU, and enables estimation of important diagnostics of molecular structure and reactivity, such as vibrational Stark measurements, halogen $\sigma$-holes, hydrogen-bond basicities and core-level shifts, as well as spin density for redox chemistry and magnetism. PET-rho-OMol25 has an accuracy close to density-functional theory, with its least reliable predictions flagged by its built-in uncertainty estimator, for most properties and classes of compounds. It can be used as a drop-in replacement for electronic-structure calculations of the density, making insightful analyses available for larger and more complex structures.

authors.name: Paolo Pegolo, Joseph W. Abbott, Michele Ceriotti

papers.title: Plasma transport by carrier electrons: Nernst advection beyond the heat-flow analogy due to kinetic stress
papers.summary: Nernst advection of magnetic fields down temperature gradients is lowered by kinetic stress from the $\underline{\underline{f}}_2$ electron distribution harmonic, which allows fluxes to stream past one another without isotropizing their lateral momentum. The long-held tie between heat-flow and Nernst advection is disrupted. When the distance between electron collisions is comparable to the magnetic field length-scale $L_B$, the kinetic stress affects magnetic transport in plasmas otherwise regarded as classical. This is from carrier electrons being deflected back and forth over the course of their trajectory. The field structure Knudsen number is defined: $Kn_B=14.8\frac{\lambda_{ei}}{L_B}\frac{Z+0.40}{Z+4.86}$, with Nernst velocity halved by kinetic effects at $Kn_B=1$. The kinetic stress is relocalized by magnetization, following the relocalization of heat-flux. Righi-Leduc heat-flow is found to be similarly suppressed by kinetic stress. The linear results of this paper are found to faithfully represent the non-linear evolution of magnetic field at a heat-front, indicating that low-$Z$ plasmas throughout magnetized-HED are demagnetized more slowly than previously anticipated.

authors.name: C. A. Walsh

papers.title: A Reconfigurable Four-State Sensor Based on Orthogonal Thermal and Chemical Stimuli
papers.summary: This article presents a novel four-state refractive index (RI) sensor based on distinct phases of palladium (Pd) and vanadium dioxide (VO$_2$), controlled by orthogonal thermal and chemical stimuli. This is a numerical, simulation-only study: all results are obtained from two-dimensional finite-element method (FEM) simulations. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first reported multi-state reconfigurable RI sensor tuned by external control. VO$_2$ serves as a phase change material (PCM) offering two thermally switchable phases with highly contrasting optical properties, while the hydrogen absorption property of Pd provides two additional phases. Combining these, four operational states are realized: (i) $\alpha$-Pd/low-$T$ VO$_2$; (ii) $\beta$-PdH$_x$/low-$T$ VO$_2$; (iii) $\alpha$-Pd/high-$T$ VO$_2$; and (iv) $\beta$-PdH$_x$/high-$T$ VO$_2$. Thermal crosstalk between Pd and VO$_2$ is mitigated through tungsten (W) doping of VO$_2$. This work further introduces conditional state sensitivity (CSS), a novel figure of merit quantifying the optical contrast between each state transition. The proposed sensor achieves a peak sensitivity of 2871 nm/RIU for the undoped reference configuration and 2798 nm/RIU for the practical W-doped device, together with a peak CSS of 16,872 nm/RIU, establishing it as a multi-state reconfigurable platform with reduced thermal crosstalk and potential applications in industrial safety monitoring and optical logic gates.

authors.name: Ashfaq Ur Rahman Ifty, Sadia Basher, Abdullah Al Zayed, Mohammad Abrar Kabir, Rakibul Hasan Sagor

papers.title: Schr\"odinger's Legacy: The Wave Function and Quantum Reality
papers.summary: The article discusses how Schr\"odinger arrived at the formulation of wave mechanics and his legacy on the philosophy of quantum mechanics, focusing in particular on the metaphysics of the wave function. Schr\"odinger's interpretation of the wave function as electron charge density is generally dismissed or presented only as a curious historical example in the literature. On a closer look, however, while this interpretation was eventually abandoned in favor of Born's statistical interpretation, Schr\"odinger's idea survived in modern realist approaches to the wave function, such as the mass-density approach and the multi-field interpretation. It also proved to be of great utility in modern techniques and approximations in quantum chemistry to compute the shape of atoms and molecules. Overall, Schr\"odinger's interpretation of the wave function and his realist understanding of quantum mechanics paved the way to modern attempts to define a clear ontology of the microscopic world, a tradition that survived the Copenhagen interpretation of Bohr and Heisenberg and that is still present today.

authors.name: Davide Romano, Massimiliano Badino

papers.title: Floquet Decomposition: Floquet Multipliers and Time-Periodic Modes from Period-Sampled Snapshot Data
papers.summary: Dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) fits one constant linear operator to a sequence of snapshots. When the dynamics, or the view of them, vary periodically, as in a parametrically excited flow or a rotating structure seen in a fixed plane, no such operator exists, and stability is decided by the Floquet multipliers, the eigenvalues of the map over one period. In the paper that introduced DMD, Schmid observed that snapshots sampled at the period of an oscillatory flow would identify the Floquet matrix. We develop that observation into a method and analyze it.
